evidence: Patch where looked up, not where defined. Break code to verify.

scenarios.title: The CI Roulette
scenarios.situation: A test fails 5% of the time in CI, passes locally. The team re-runs failures. Nobody investigates.
choices: Re-run until green; it's probably fine.

Quarantine immediately: mark it (pytest -m flaky, separate suite), assign an owner and deadline, and keep it out of the blocking suite. Flaky tests train the team to ignore red — then real failures hide in the noise. Common causes: time dependence, shared state, real network, unseeded randomness. Fix the cause, not the re-run button.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. A flaky test is worse than no test: it consumes trust in the whole suite. The quarantine workflow (separate, owned, deadlined) preserves signal while the cause is fixed. 'Re-run until green' normalizes red; the 5% failure WILL coincide with a real regression eventually, and nobody will notice. Flakiness is a bug with a distinctive signature — investigate it like one.
scenarios.hint: What does the team learn from re-running: the cause, or to ignore red?
evidence: Out of the blocking suite, owned, deadlined. Re-runs normalize red.

scenarios.title: The Mock-Only Suite
scenarios.situation: All tests pass with mocks. Production breaks: the real S3 API paginates differently than the mock assumed. The mock encoded the team's misunderstanding.
choices: Integration tests against the real (or faithful fake like moto/localstack): mocks encode assumptions, and wrong assumptions mock green. The seam — your code vs the real service — needs at least one test that touches reality. Contract tests are the lighter alternative: verify against the provider's spec.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mocks test your code against your beliefs; integration tests test your beliefs against reality. Pagination, error formats, auth flows — the details mocks get wrong are exactly the details that break production. The testing pyramid needs its middle: enough integration to cover the seams, fast enough to run. moto/localstack give S3-faithful fakes without AWS bills.
scenarios.hint: What did the mock encode: reality or the team's assumption?
evidence: Mocks encode beliefs. Integration tests check them against reality.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Bug
scenarios.situation: A billing test passes all day, fails at midnight: it uses datetime.now() and the date rolled over mid-test-run.
choices: Inject the clock: pass now() as a parameter (or a clock object), and freeze it in tests (freezegun). Tests must control time — real time in tests is non-determinism. The midnight failure is the signature: the test depended on wall-clock state it didn't control.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Time is an implicit input — tests must make it explicit and controllable. The inject-the-clock pattern (default now=datetime.now, override in tests) plus freezegun covers it. 'Don't run at midnight' schedules around the bug; the bug is depending on uncontrolled state. Time, randomness, and I/O are the unholy trinity of flakiness — control all three.
scenarios.hint: What input did the test depend on without controlling?
evidence: Tests control time. freezegun + parameterize now().

scenarios.title: The Inverted Pyramid
scenarios.situation: A team has 10 unit tests and 500 end-to-end tests. The suite takes 3 hours, flakes constantly, and developers skip it.
choices: More e2e; they catch real bugs.

Rebuild the pyramid: many fast unit tests (the base), fewer integration tests (the middle), few e2e tests (the tip). Move logic down — the e2e tests are testing business rules that belong in unit tests. The 3-hour flaky suite is worse than no suite: it's a tax everyone evades.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). The inverted pyramid fails on every axis: slow (3h feedback), flaky (e2e has the most moving parts), and skipped (so it catches nothing). The fix is moving tests DOWN: extract the logic e2e covers into unit-testable functions, keep e2e for the critical paths only. Speed and reliability are what make suites actually run.
scenarios.hint: Why do developers skip the suite?
evidence: Many unit, some integration, few e2e. Move logic down.

scenarios.title: Mock vs Fake
scenarios.situation: A test needs a database. Options: mock every cursor call, or use a FakeDatabase (in-memory dict with the same interface).
choices: When interactions are complex: fakes have BEHAVIOR (insert then select returns the row), mocks have EXPECTATIONS (assert called_with). Multi-step flows with a mock become brittle expectation-scripts; with a fake they read naturally. Rule: mock at simple boundaries, fake complex collaborators, use the real thing when cheap (SQLite).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The mock/fake/real spectrum trades fidelity for speed: mocks (fast, brittle for complex flows), fakes (behavioral, great for stateful collaborators), real (slowest, truest — SQLite/testcontainers). The failure mode is mocking complex interactions: the test becomes a mirror of the implementation, breaking on every refactor while proving nothing about behavior.
scenarios.hint: Does the test need expectations or behavior?
evidence: Mocks: expectations. Fakes: behavior. Real: truth. Pick by fidelity need.

scenarios.title: The 100% Illusion
scenarios.situation: Coverage is 100%. A bug ships: an untested branch combination (two flags interacting) that no test exercised.
scenarios.prompt: What does this show about coverage?
choices: Coverage measures which LINES ran, not which BEHAVIORS were verified: 100% line coverage with weak assertions (or no assertions on combinations) is the illusion of safety. The fix: assertion quality (mutation testing measures it), plus combinatorial thinking (the bug was in the interaction, not the lines). Coverage is necessary, not sufficient.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Line coverage answers 'did it run?' — not 'was it checked?' A test that calls the function and asserts nothing gives coverage without verification. Mutation testing (mutate the code, see if tests catch it) measures assertion strength. And combinatorial bugs need combinatorial tests (pairwise, property-based). Coverage gates the minimum; it never certifies correctness.
scenarios.hint: Did the lines run, or were they verified?
evidence: Lines ran ≠ behaviors verified. Mutation-test the assertions.

domains.name: Exam & Interview Prep
domains.summary: How Python systems roles are hired: live coding, systems design, debugging scenarios, and behavioral rounds.

scenarios.title: Explain the GIL
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Explain the GIL and when it matters.'
choices: 'It's a lock that makes Python slow.'

The GIL serializes CPython bytecode execution — one thread runs Python code at a time. It matters for CPU-bound threads (no speedup; use multiprocessing/C extensions/free-threading); it doesn't matter for I/O-bound (threads yield during waits) or single-threaded code. The trade: it makes CPython fast and C extensions simple. Answer with the decision rule, not just the definition.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The complete answer has four parts: mechanism (bytecode serialization), when it bites (CPU-bound threads), when it doesn't (I/O-bound, single-thread), and the escapes (multiprocessing, native, free-threading). Interviewers want the decision rule — 'threads for I/O, processes for CPU' — WITH the mechanism behind it. Definition without implications is trivia.
scenarios.hint: When does it bite, and what's the escape?
evidence: Mechanism + when it bites + escapes. Decision rule with reasons.

scenarios.title: Tell Me About a Deadlock
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a deadlock or race you debugged.'
choices: The physics: what deadlocked (pipe buffer? lock order? GIL?), the diagnostic signature (size-dependent hang? nondeterministic count?), the tool that found it, and the structural fix — plus what you changed to prevent the class. 'I added a lock' is weak; 'I eliminated the sharing' is strong. Stories are graded on mechanism + fix depth.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. War stories are graded like incident reviews: precise mechanism, diagnostic reasoning, fix depth (structural > symptomatic), and the class-level lesson. 'Never hit one' fails credibility for a systems role; blaming the library fails ownership. The bug ledger from this course IS the story bank — each entry is a rehearsed answer.
scenarios.hint: What was the mechanism, and what did you change structurally?
evidence: Precise physics, diagnostic signature, structural fix, class lesson.

scenarios.title: Design a Rate Limiter
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Design a rate limiter. 10 minutes.'
choices: Fixed window is fine; skip details.

Clarify (per-user? distributed? algorithm: token bucket vs fixed window?), implement the single-process core (token bucket with time-based refill — 15 lines), then discuss distribution (Redis + Lua for atomicity), edge cases (clock skew, burst), and testing. Working core first, distributed second — the single-node solution proves the algorithm; the discussion proves the systems thinking.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The 10-minute design: clarify scope, build the core (token bucket is 15 lines and shows the algorithm), then scale the discussion (distributed atomicity via Redis+Lua, edge cases). Starting distributed wastes the 10 minutes on infrastructure before proving the algorithm. 'Use a library' abdicates the question — they want YOUR design reasoning.
scenarios.hint: What proves first: the algorithm or the infrastructure?
evidence: Single-process algorithm first, distributed discussion second.

scenarios.title: The Subprocess Question
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Your script shells out to a command with user input. Walk me through the risks.'
choices: Shell injection (shell=True/f-string + user input = code execution), the fix (argv list, shell=False), plus the adjacent risks: unbounded hangs (timeout=), pipe deadlocks (communicate), silent failures (check=True), and environment leaks (minimal env). The question tests whether 'subprocess' means one API call or a risk surface — seniors see the surface.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The complete answer maps the whole risk surface: injection (the headline), hangs, deadlocks, silent failures, env leaks — each with its mitigation. 'Use shell=False' alone is correct but shallow; the interviewer is probing whether you see the adjacent failure modes. Sanitization is the weaker fix (bypassable); no-shell is structural.
scenarios.hint: Is it one risk or a surface?
evidence: Injection + hangs + deadlocks + silent fails + env. Mitigate each.

scenarios.title: Why asyncio?
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Why asyncio over threads for 10k connections?'
choices: Resource physics: 10k threads = 10k stacks (~80MB+ just for stacks) + scheduler contention + GIL; asyncio = one thread, coroutines are tiny state machines, waits overlap with near-zero overhead. The trade: asyncio demands non-blocking discipline (one time.sleep freezes all); threads tolerate blocking but don't scale to 10k. Numbers, not adjectives.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The precise answer quantifies: thread stacks (~8MB virtual each), context-switch cost, vs coroutine overhead (KBs). And it names asyncio's price: the non-blocking contract — one blocking call stalls everything. 'Always better' fails the trade-off test; the senior answer picks by connection count and blocking tolerance, with numbers.
scenarios.hint: What does 10k threads cost vs 10k coroutines?
evidence: Thread stacks vs coroutine state. Name asyncio's price too.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Story
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a production incident you owned.'
choices: STAR with systems depth: the symptom and stakes, YOUR specific actions (not the team's), the diagnostic method (hypothesis → test), the fix (structural, not just the revert), the follow-up (runbook, alert, test that prevents recurrence), and the numbers (MTTR, impact). Ownership + method + systemic fix + metrics.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). Incident stories test ownership and learning: 'I' actions (not 'we'), method (not luck), structural fix (not just mitigation), and prevention (the test/alert/runbook that followed). Heroics ('I stayed up 20 hours') signal poor process; the systemic follow-up signals seniority. Numbers make it checkable.
scenarios.hint: What did YOU do, and what prevents recurrence?
evidence: Your actions, your method, the structural fix, the metrics.

scenarios.title: Multiprocessing vs asyncio?
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'When would you pick multiprocessing over asyncio?'
choices: CPU-bound → multiprocessing (real parallelism past the GIL); I/O-bound many-connection → asyncio (scales connections); I/O-bound few-task → threads (simpler). Plus the costs: multiprocessing = pickling + memory + complexity; asyncio = non-blocking discipline. The rule is workload physics, and the senior adds: 'measure — the profile decides, not the fashion.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The decision tree from the concurrency domain, applied live: waiting vs computing, how many concurrent, what costs. Each option's price named (pickling, discipline, complexity). 'Measure' is the credibility closer — it shows the rule is empirical, not tribal. Interviewers want the tree, not the favorite.
scenarios.hint: What's the workload: waiting or computing?

domains.name: Mock Assessment: Timed Trial
domains.description: A timed, mixed-domain final assessment simulating interview conditions: live coding, systems design, debugging scenarios, and trade-off questions from every domain. Take it mid-course as a diagnostic and again at the end.

lessons.title: Python for Systems Programming — Core concepts
concepts: subprocess replaces os.system for running external commands: pass an argument list with shell=False to avoid shell injection, use capture_output=True and text=True for readable output, check=True to raise on nonzero exit, and timeout= to bound hangs.

asyncio runs many I/O-bound tasks on one thread: coroutines await each other cooperatively, the event loop switches during I/O waits, and create_task + gather overlap waits. It never speeds up CPU-bound work — the GIL still serializes bytecode.

Packaging is metadata plus a build backend: pyproject.toml's [project] table (PEP 621) declares name, version, requires-python, dependencies, and console entry points; pip installs from it, and virtual environments keep each project's dependency set isolated.

Profiling precedes optimization: cProfile measures where time actually goes (tottime vs cumtime), and the fix is usually algorithmic or structural (hoist repeated work, reduce I/O) rather than micro-tuning. Measure before and after every change.

Systems code must handle the unhappy paths: subprocess calls can hang (use timeouts), children can outlive parents (handle SIGTERM and reap with wait), queues can deadlock (bounded queues need a live consumer), and resources need deterministic cleanup (context managers, try/finally).

example.code:
import asyncio, sys

async def fetch_one(client, url):
    async with client.get(url) as resp:
        return url, resp.status

async def main(urls):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:   # 3.11+: structured concurrency
        tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch_one(u)) for u in urls]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

asyncio.run(main(sys.argv[1:]))
example.walkthrough: TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) schedules every fetch as a task so the network waits overlap, and it waits for all of them — cancelling stragglers if one fails. asyncio.run builds and tears down the event loop; the whole program stays on one thread.

pitfalls: Common trap: shell=True with any user-influenced string — injection, not just a style issue.
Common trap: awaiting coroutines one-by-one in a loop and wondering why nothing is concurrent.
Common trap: using asyncio for CPU-bound number crunching — threads don't help either under the GIL; use multiprocessing.
Common trap: optimizing before profiling — cProfile first, or you will speed up code that doesn't matter.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Python Systems move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Python for Systems Programming
concepts: Python for Systems Programming is a multi-step process within Python for Systems Programming: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Python for Systems Programming to the broader Python for Systems Programming ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Python for Systems Programming begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Python for Systems Programming. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Python for Systems Programming as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Python for Systems Programming flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp is organized as domains (major areas). Each domain holds lessons (concept briefings with runnable Python), scenarios (graded design and debugging decisions), and labs (hands-on scripts with verifiable outputs).
The intended loop: read a lesson, run its example code yourself, attempt scenarios closed-book, then do the lab. Systems programming is learned at the terminal — the REPL is your laboratory.

Every lesson example is runnable: copy it, run it, break it, fix it. The scenarios test the decisions you will face in interviews and on-call: concurrency choices, failure handling, performance trade-offs.
The mock-assessment domain is a timed final; capstone-build guides you to ship a production-grade systems tool (a log shipper / process supervisor) in three phases.

example.code:
A 90-minute study block:
  0:00-0:20  read the lesson; run every example in a REPL
  0:20-0:45  scenarios closed-book, committing to each answer
  0:45-1:20  lab: write the script, verify the checks
  1:20-1:30  error log: one line per miss + the fix command
example.walkthrough: Running the examples is non-negotiable: the difference between reading about the GIL and watching threads not speed up is the difference between trivia and understanding. Break things deliberately.

pitfalls: Reading code without running it. The terminal is the teacher.
Peeking at answers before committing. The commitment is the training.
Skipping labs because the code 'looked clear.' Clarity is not competence.
lessons.try_it: Set up a scratch directory ~/pylab with a virtualenv; every lab lives there.

lessons.title: Your Study Strategy: Code-First Learning
concepts: One concept, one script: after each lesson, write a 20-line script proving the concept (spawn the subprocess, fill the pipe, deadlock the threads on purpose). Unproven concepts evaporate.
Read the standard library like documentation, not magic: subprocess, os, socket, asyncio, logging, argparse — the docs are the textbook, and every lesson maps to a module.
Interleave domains: study concurrency alongside network programming — the job mixes them (an async TCP server), so your practice should too.
Keep a bug ledger: every scenario miss and lab failure becomes a one-line entry (symptom → root cause → fix). Review it before each session; it is your personal runbook.

example.code:
Bug-ledger entry:
  SYMPTOM: subprocess hangs on large output
  CAUSE: pipe buffer filled; child blocked writing, parent blocked waiting
  FIX: use communicate() or read stdout incrementally — never wait()
        before draining the pipe
example.walkthrough: The ledger converts each failure into a searchable fix. Senior engineers are not people who never hit the pipe deadlock — they are people who hit it once and wrote it down.

pitfalls: Tutorial-hopping without writing code. Watching is not doing.
Memorizing APIs instead of patterns. Patterns (drain the pipe, bound the queue) transfer; signatures do not.
Avoiding the hard domains (concurrency, networking). The interviews live there.
lessons.try_it: Write your first bug-ledger entry after the orientation scenarios.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: The Thirteen Domains
concepts: Foundations arc: subprocess-automation, filesystem-operations, and config-management — how Python talks to the OS, the disk, and its own configuration.
Systems arc: network-programming, concurrency-systems, and performance-profiling — sockets, threads/processes/asyncio, and making it fast (with the GIL's honest limits).
Production arc: logging-monitoring, cli-development, and testing-systems — the difference between a script and a tool: observability, interface, and tests.
Capstone arc: pse-exam-prep collects interview strategy; mock-assessment is the timed trial; capstone-build ships a real systems tool in three phases.

example.code:
Roadmap:
  start-here -> subprocess-automation -> filesystem-operations
      -> config-management -> network-programming -> concurrency-systems
      -> performance-profiling -> logging-monitoring -> cli-development
      -> testing-systems -> pse-exam-prep -> mock-assessment -> capstone-build
example.walkthrough: The order is load-bearing: concurrency needs the process model (subprocess), networking needs byte handling, and the capstone needs all of them. Skipping ahead borrows understanding you have not earned.

pitfalls: Starting with asyncio before understanding processes and threads. The event loop is not magic.
Treating testing as a final chapter. Test each domain's labs as you go.
Saving the mock for 'when ready.' Take it early as a diagnostic.
lessons.try_it: Mark the two domains you know least and schedule them first — weakness-first ordering.

lessons.title: Labs, Scenarios, and the Mock Assessment
concepts: Labs give steps plus checks: the checks name the verifiable output (a timing comparison, an exit code, a log line). They are self-verification — run the command, match the pattern.
Scenarios carry objectives (what is tested), mins (budget like an interview), evidence (the reference fact), and a hint. Commit to an answer before reading the hint.
The mock assessment simulates interview pressure: mixed-domain questions, code reading, trade-off decisions, no hints, strict time. Take it twice — mid-course and at the end.
The capstone ships a real tool: a log shipper / process supervisor with CLI, config, logging, tests, and packaging. It is the artifact you demo — 'I built this' beats 'I studied this.'

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  120 minutes, no notes, domains mixed
  -> score -> log every miss in the bug ledger
  -> re-run the failed lab commands by hand
  -> re-study only the missed distinctions
example.walkthrough: Two timed runs train retrieval under pressure — the interview condition. The bug ledger turns each miss into a drill; the re-run turns the drill into muscle memory.

pitfalls: Using hints as a first resort.
Treating the capstone as optional. It is the interview artifact.
Reviewing only correct answers. The misses are the curriculum.
lessons.try_it: Run one lab from the subprocess domain today to feel the format under no pressure.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 1 — Core Engine: Tail, Parse, Ship
concepts: Define the tool: logship watches log files (like tail -F), parses lines, and ships JSON records to a destination (stdout/file/HTTP). One binary, one config file, one job.
Core loop: inotify/watchdog for file events (not polling), offset tracking (resume after restart — store offsets in a state file), backpressure (bounded queue; drop or block policy explicit).
Parsing: regex or structured parsers per input, with a dead-letter path for unparsable lines. Unparsable lines are data too — count them, sample them, alert on spikes.
Done criteria for phase 1: survives log rotation, survives restart (offsets), handles 10k lines/sec without loss, dead-letter rate visible. Measure, don't hope.

example.code:
from watchdog.observers import Observer
from watchdog.events import FileSystemEventHandler
import json, re

LINE = re.compile(r'(?P<ts>\S+) (?P<level>\w+) (?P<msg>.*)')

class Handler(FileSystemEventHandler):
    def on_modified(self, event):
        for line in read_new_lines(event.src_path):  # offset-tracked
            m = LINE.match(line)
            ship(m.groupdict() if m else dead_letter(line))
example.walkthrough: The offset tracking is the reliability core: without it, every restart re-ships or loses lines. State the invariant explicitly — 'every byte shipped exactly once across restarts' — then design to it. Rotation handling (inode tracking) is the classic edge case.

pitfalls: Polling instead of inotify. Latency and CPU waste; rotation races.
No offset persistence. Restarts re-ship or lose — pick your data loss.
Unbounded queues. Backpressure must be a designed policy, not an OOM.
lessons.try_it: Write the invariant list for your shipper: exactly-once across restart, rotation, and backpressure.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 2 — Production Hardening
concepts: CLI: argparse/click interface (logship ship --config, logship validate, logship status). Every operation scriptable; --help complete. The CLI is the tool's UI.
Config: TOML/YAML file with schema validation at startup (fail fast on bad config — never fail at 3 AM on a typo). Env-var overrides for secrets (12-factor).
Logging and observability: structured JSON logs to stderr, a /health endpoint or status command, Prometheus-style counters (lines shipped, parse errors, queue depth). The tool must be monitorable.
Signals and shutdown: SIGTERM → drain the queue, flush offsets, exit cleanly. A shipper that loses data on deploy is a data-loss machine with a config file.

example.code:
import signal, sys

shutdown = False
def handle_term(signum, frame):
    global shutdown
    shutdown = True          # stop taking new work
    # main loop: while not shutdown: ...
    # then: drain queue, flush offsets, close files, exit 0
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle_term)
example.walkthrough: The signal handler does the minimum: set a flag. All cleanup happens in the main loop's normal flow — handlers that do real work (I/O, locks) risk reentrancy bugs. Flag-and-drain is the pattern; async-signal-safety is the reason.

pitfalls: Config typos failing at 3 AM. Validate at startup, fail fast.
SIGKILL-only shutdowns. Data loss on every deploy.
Unstructured logs. The shipper's own logs must be shippable.
lessons.try_it: Send SIGTERM to your shipper mid-load; verify zero loss and clean offset flush.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 3 — Tests, Packaging, Docs
concepts: Tests: unit (parser edge cases), integration (real files, rotation, restart recovery), and a chaos test (kill -9 mid-ship, verify no loss/duplication beyond policy). The chaos test is the credibility.
Packaging: pyproject.toml, pinned dependencies, a Docker image (distroless/slim), and a systemd unit example. 'pip install logship' should work from a clean machine.
Docs: README with quickstart (5 min to shipping), config reference, runbook for the three known failure modes (rotation race, backpressure, parse-error spike), and the invariant list.
Demo: tail a live log, rotate it, kill -9 the shipper, restart — show zero loss. The demo IS the interview artifact; record it.

example.code:
# chaos test sketch (pytest):
# 1. start shipper on a log stream (subprocess)
# 2. write 50k lines; kill -9 at a random point
# 3. restart shipper; let it drain
# 4. assert shipped == written (exactly-once) or duplicates <= policy
# 5. repeat 20x (flakes here are real bugs)
example.walkthrough: The kill -9 loop is the honesty test: it exercises the exact-once invariant under the worst case. Flakes in this test are not test bugs — they are shipper bugs wearing a test costume. Fix the shipper, not the test.

pitfalls: Skipping the chaos test. Unproven invariants are wishes.
Unpinned dependencies. 'Works on my machine' as a distribution strategy.
Docs without the invariant list. Users cannot operate what they cannot reason about.
lessons.try_it: Record the demo: live tail, rotation, kill -9, restart, zero loss. Watch it once; cut ruthlessly.

lessons.title: Python Systems — The OS Interface
concepts: Python's systems power is its OS interface: os, sys, subprocess, socket, signal — thin, honest wrappers over POSIX. Systems Python is mostly orchestrating what the OS already does.
Everything is a file descriptor: files, sockets, pipes share the read/write/close interface. Code that works on fds generically (select, sendfile) composes across domains.

Bytes vs str is the systems boundary: the OS speaks bytes (filenames, socket data, subprocess I/O); Python 3 forces you to decode explicitly. Encoding bugs are the tax on crossing the boundary carelessly.
Errors are values: OSError with errno tells you exactly what failed (ENOENT, EACCES, EPIPE). Catch specifically, handle deliberately — except OSError: pass is how outages hide.

example.walkthrough: Specific errno handling turns 'it failed' into 'it failed because' — the difference between a mystery and a runbook entry. The else: raise is the discipline: handle what you understand, propagate what you don't.

pitfalls: Bare except: pass. Outages hide here.
Treating filenames as str always. Surrogateescape exists for a reason; bytes are truth.
Ignoring errno. The number IS the diagnosis.
lessons.try_it: Write a pidfile reader that distinguishes not-running, permission-denied, and corrupt-pidfile.

lessons.title: Python Systems — Processes and Signals
concepts: A process is an isolated address space; fork/exec (via subprocess) creates them. Python's multiprocessing sidesteps the GIL with real parallelism — at the cost of pickling overhead and complexity.

Signals are the OS's notifications: SIGTERM (please stop), SIGKILL (stop now), SIGHUP (reload?), SIGCHLD (child changed). Handlers must be fast and reentrant — set a flag, do the work in the main loop.
Zombie processes: children that exited but were never wait()ed. The parent must reap (waitpid) or the zombies accumulate. subprocess handles this for you; raw os.fork does not — reap your children.

Daemonization done right: double-fork is folklore; prefer a supervisor (systemd) managing a foreground process. Your program should run in the foreground and handle SIGTERM — let init do the daemonizing.

example.code:
import signal
stop = False
def on_term(signum, frame):
    global stop
    stop = False if False else True  # set the flag; nothing else
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_term)
# main loop: while not stop: work()
# then: drain, flush, close, exit 0
example.walkthrough: The handler's minimalism is the point: signal handlers run in a fragile context (interrupted syscalls, no locks). Set the flag; the main loop — with its normal error handling — does the dignified shutdown.

pitfalls: Doing I/O in signal handlers. Reentrancy bugs are the worst kind.
Ignoring SIGTERM. The orchestrator will SIGKILL you; drain gracefully instead.
Double-fork daemons in 2026. systemd exists; foreground + SIGTERM is the contract.
lessons.try_it: Write a worker that handles SIGTERM by finishing the current item then exiting cleanly.

lessons.title: Python Systems — The GIL, Honestly
concepts: The GIL serializes CPython bytecode: one thread executes Python code at a time. It makes single-threaded code fast and C extensions simple — at the cost of thread parallelism for CPU-bound work.

The decision tree: I/O-bound (network, disk waits) → threads or asyncio (waits overlap); CPU-bound (compute) → multiprocessing or native code (real parallelism). Misdiagnosing which you have is the classic error.
Free-threading (PEP 703, 3.13+) is changing this: no-GIL builds allow true thread parallelism, but C extensions must be thread-safe. Know your interpreter build before assuming.
Measure, don't assume: cProfile + a threaded experiment tells you in minutes whether threads help. The GIL's effects are workload-specific — theory predicts poorly, measurement predicts well.

example.code:
import time, threading
def burn():
    sum(i*i for i in range(10**7))  # CPU-bound
t0=time.perf_counter()
threads=[threading.Thread(target=burn) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]; [t.join() for t in threads]
print(f'threads: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f}s')
# compare vs sequential: often NO speedup (GIL). Now try multiprocessing.
example.walkthrough: The experiment is the lesson: run it, see threads stall on CPU work, then swap in multiprocessing and watch it scale. Ten minutes at the terminal beats ten pages of theory about the GIL.

pitfalls: Threads for CPU-bound work. The GIL says no.
Processes for I/O-bound work. Pickling overhead for no benefit.
Assuming free-threading everywhere. Check sys._is_gil_enabled() on 3.13+.
lessons.try_it: Run the burn test with threads vs processes; record the speedup ratio.

lessons.title: Python Systems — Packaging and Distribution
concepts: pyproject.toml is the modern manifest: build system, dependencies, entry points, all declarative. setup.py is legacy — know it exists, don't write new ones.
Virtualenvs isolate: one project, one environment, no system-Python pollution. uv/pip-tools pin the full tree (lockfile) — 'works on my machine' dies with pinned, hashed dependencies.
Entry points make CLIs installable: [project.scripts] logship = 'logship.cli:main' — pip install gives you a real command. Scripts without entry points are not tools.
Distribute as containers for services, wheels for libraries, and single binaries (PyInstaller/Nuitka) for agents that must run anywhere. Match the artifact to the deployment.

example.code:
[project]
name = 'logship'
version = '0.3.0'
description = 'Log shipper with exactly-once semantics'
requires-python = '>=3.11'
dependencies = ['watchdog>=4.0', 'click>=8.0']
[project.scripts]
logship = 'logship.cli:main'
example.walkthrough: The manifest's completeness is the installability: name, version, python floor, pinned deps, entry point. Anyone should pip-install from a clean machine and get a working command — that is the bar.

pitfalls: Unpinned dependencies. Upstream changes break your users silently.
System-Python installs. One project's upgrade breaks another's runtime.
No entry points. 'Clone the repo and run the script' is not distribution.
lessons.try_it: Package a scratch tool with pyproject + entry point; install it in a fresh venv.

lessons.title: Python Systems — Debugging Production Python
concepts: faulthandler: dump tracebacks on timeout or signal — the first tool for hung production processes. faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(60) turns 'it's stuck' into 'it's stuck HERE.'
py-spy: sample a running process without restarting it (no code changes, no instrumentation). The flame graph shows where time goes — production profiling without the observer effect.
Post-mortem: traceback + locals at the crash site. Log the exception with context (request ID, inputs hash) — 'it crashed' is not debuggable; 'it crashed on input X in state Y' is.
Reproduce locally with the same data: production bugs that cannot be reproduced are investigated with logs and traces, not guesses. Invest in log context before you need it.

example.code:
import faulthandler, signal
faulthandler.register(signal.SIGUSR1)  # kill -USR1 <pid> dumps traceback
faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(300, exit=True)  # watchdog: stuck >5min?
# py-spy: py-spy dump --pid <pid>  (no restart, no code change)
example.walkthrough: SIGUSR1-as-debugger is the production pattern: the process runs normally, and on demand you get its exact stack. It costs nothing until used — which is why it belongs in every long-running service from day one.

pitfalls: No faulthandler in production. Hung processes stay mysteries.
Guessing at production bugs. Logs and traces first, theories second.
Restarting to 'fix' hangs. The hang will return; the traceback would have told you why.
lessons.try_it: Add faulthandler to a long-running script; trigger a dump and read the stacks.

lessons.title: Python Systems — The Systems Mindset
concepts: Think in resources: every fd, socket, thread, and byte has a lifecycle — open/close, bind/unbind, acquire/release. Leaks are lifecycle bugs; review code for the close, not just the open.
Think in failure modes: what happens when the disk fills, the network partitions, the peer dies mid-write? The happy path is 10% of systems code; the other 90% is the failure modes.
Think in invariants: 'every byte shipped exactly once,' 'no unbounded queues,' 'shutdown always drains.' Invariants turn code review from style-checking into correctness-checking.
Think in observability: if you cannot see it, you cannot operate it. Metrics, structured logs, and health checks are not features — they are the preconditions for running the thing.

example.code:
Review checklist (systems code):
  [ ] every open has a close (context managers?)
  [ ] every queue is bounded with a full-policy
  [ ] every network call has a timeout
  [ ] SIGTERM drains cleanly (no data loss)
  [ ] failure modes enumerated: disk full? peer dead? slow consumer?
  [ ] metrics/logs expose the invariants
example.walkthrough: The checklist converts the mindset into a repeatable review: each item is a bug class that has caused real outages. Run it on your capstone before the demo — the interviewer certainly will.

pitfalls: Reviewing style, missing lifecycle. The leak is not in the formatting.
Happy-path-only code. The 90% is the job.
Observability as an afterthought. Unobservable systems are unoperable.
lessons.try_it: Run the checklist on your capstone; fix the first failure it finds.

lessons.title: subprocess.run: The Right Default
concepts: subprocess.run is the high-level API: run a command, wait, get the result. Prefer it over Popen unless you need streaming or interaction — most scripts do not.
Always pass an argument list with shell=False: run(['grep', pattern, file]) — no shell parsing, no injection. shell=True is the exception needing justification, never the default.
check=True raises CalledProcessError on nonzero exit — fail fast instead of silently continuing with garbage. capture_output=True + text=True gives you readable stdout/stderr.
timeout= bounds hangs: run(cmd, timeout=30) raises TimeoutExpired. Every external command can hang; unbounded waits are how scripts become zombies.

example.code:
import subprocess
r = subprocess.run(
    ['git', 'log', '--oneline', '-5'],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=30)
print(r.stdout)          # decoded str, not bytes
# r.returncode == 0 guaranteed by check=True
# on failure: CalledProcessError with .cmd, .returncode, .stderr
example.walkthrough: The four flags are the safe default shape: list args (no shell), check (fail fast), capture+text (readable output), timeout (bounded). Memorize this call shape — it is 90% of subprocess usage.

pitfalls: os.system / os.popen. Legacy, shell-injectable, no structured errors.
shell=True with f-strings. Code injection waiting for user input.
No timeout. The hung subprocess outlives your patience and your pager.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one os.system call in your codebase with the safe run() shape.

lessons.title: Popen: Streaming and Interaction
concepts: Popen is the low-level primitive: start the process, interact with its pipes, manage its lifecycle. Reach for it when run() cannot stream or interact.
communicate() is the safe interaction: writes stdin, drains stdout/stderr, waits — all without deadlock. The rule: with PIPEs, communicate() or stream; never bare wait().
Streaming large output: iterate over p.stdout line by line instead of reading it all — constant memory regardless of output size. The 10GB log file test.
stdin piping: feed input via communicate(input=data) or p.stdin.write + close. Close stdin when done — the child may be waiting for EOF to finish.

example.code:
import subprocess
p = subprocess.Popen(['grep', 'ERROR'],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
out, _ = p.communicate(input=log_text, timeout=30)  # safe: drains + waits
# streaming alternative for huge outputs:
# for line in p.stdout: process(line)
# p.wait()  # safe AFTER stdout is exhausted
example.walkthrough: communicate() is the deadlock-free pattern because it pumps the pipes concurrently with waiting. The streaming form works because the parent consumes as the child produces — the pipe never fills. Both respect the same physics: someone must read.

pitfalls: wait() before reading a PIPE. The classic deadlock.
read() on huge outputs. Memory grows with the child's verbosity.
Forgetting to close stdin. The child waits for EOF; you wait for the child.
lessons.try_it: Write a script that greps a 1GB file via streaming; verify constant memory.

lessons.title: Exit Codes, Signals, and Timeouts
concepts: Exit codes are the process's last words: 0 = success, nonzero = failure, 128+N = killed by signal N (137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM). Read them; they diagnose.
TimeoutExpired is not the end: on timeout, kill the process (p.kill()), then communicate() again to reap it — otherwise it becomes a zombie or keeps running detached.
Distinguish failure types: CalledProcessError (command failed), TimeoutExpired (hung), FileNotFoundError (command missing). Each needs different handling — retry the hung, alert the missing.
Timeouts compose: per-command timeouts inside an overall deadline. A pipeline of 10 commands each with 30s timeouts can still run 5 minutes — bound the whole thing too.

example.code:
import subprocess
try:
    r = subprocess.run(['rsync', '-a', src, dst],
                       capture_output=True, text=True,
                       timeout=300, check=True)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    alert('rsync hung >5m')       # kill already attempted by run()
    raise
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    log.error('rsync failed', code=e.returncode, err=e.stderr[-500:])
    raise
example.walkthrough: The exception taxonomy is the handling guide: timeout → the command hung (alert, investigate the hang); nonzero exit → the command failed (log stderr, maybe retry); missing binary → the environment is wrong (fix the image). Different causes, different runbooks.

pitfalls: Catching all exceptions identically. Timeout and failure need different responses.
No kill on timeout with Popen. The hung child survives your script.
Ignoring 137/143. Signal-deaths have different meanings than exit-1.
lessons.try_it: Write a wrapper that runs a command with timeout, kills on expiry, and reports the failure class.

lessons.title: Process Supervision Patterns
concepts: Supervision = keep it running: restart on crash, with backoff (don't hot-loop a crashing process), and a max-restart cap (crash-looping forever helps nobody).
Backoff strategy: exponential with jitter (1s, 2s, 4s... + random) — prevents thundering-herd restarts when a dependency flaps. Constant 1s restarts are a DoS on yourself.
Health beyond 'is it running': liveness (process alive) vs readiness (serving correctly). A process can be alive and wedged — supervise the health check, not just the PID.
Prefer real supervisors (systemd, supervisord, Kubernetes) over hand-rolled loops. Write the supervision policy as config; reserve custom code for custom health logic.

example.code:
import subprocess, time, random
backoff = 1
while True:
    p = subprocess.Popen(['./worker'])
    rc = p.wait()
    log.warning('worker exited', code=rc)
    if not healthy_enough_to_restart():
        break  # crash loop cap: page a human
    time.sleep(backoff + random.uniform(0, 1))  # jittered backoff
    backoff = min(backoff * 2, 60)
example.walkthrough: The loop's three controls are the supervision policy: backoff (don't hammer), jitter (don't synchronize), cap (don't loop forever). Everything else — health checks, alerting — builds on these three.

pitfalls: Restart without backoff. Hot-looping a crashing process is self-DoS.
No crash cap. Infinite restarts hide the real problem forever.
Supervising the PID, not the health. Alive != working.
lessons.try_it: Implement the supervisor loop with backoff, jitter, and a crash cap; test with a flaky worker.

lessons.title: Pipelines and Redirection in Python
concepts: Shell pipelines (a | b | c) in Python: chain Popen objects, wiring stdout to stdin — or use subprocess.run with input= for simple cases. Avoid shell=True for the pipeline.
The pattern: p1 = Popen(['prog1'], stdout=PIPE); p2 = Popen(['prog2'], stdin=p1.stdout, stdout=PIPE); p1.stdout.close(); out = p2.communicate()[0]. The close() lets p1 get SIGPIPE if p2 exits early.
Redirection: stdout=open('out.log','w') writes directly to the file — no Python-side buffering, no memory growth. stderr=subprocess.STDOUT merges streams when order matters.
Prefer Python to pipelines when logic grows: a 5-stage shell pipeline with error handling is clearer as Python functions. The shell is for composition; Python is for logic.

example.code:
import subprocess
p1 = subprocess.Popen(['cat', 'big.log'], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
p2 = subprocess.Popen(['grep', 'ERROR'], stdin=p1.stdout, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
p1.stdout.close()  # allow SIGPIPE if grep exits early
out, _ = p2.communicate()
# equivalent shell: cat big.log | grep ERROR  (but no shell involved)
example.walkthrough: The p1.stdout.close() is the subtle correctness: without it, p1 never receives SIGPIPE when p2 exits early (the parent still holds the fd open), so p1 runs to completion pointlessly. Parent-held pipe ends defeat the pipeline's early-exit semantics.

pitfalls: shell=True for pipelines. Injection risk for composition convenience.
Forgetting the close(). Pipelines lose their early-exit behavior.
Giant pipelines in shell with error handling. Python is clearer past 3 stages.
lessons.try_it: Build a 3-stage Python pipeline; verify early exit propagates SIGPIPE correctly.

lessons.title: pathlib: Paths Done Right
concepts: pathlib.Path replaces os.path string surgery: p / 'sub' / 'file.txt' joins correctly on every OS, and methods (exists(), read_text(), glob()) hang off the object. Stop concatenating strings.
Resolve vs absolute: .resolve() normalizes symlinks and .. (use for identity), .absolute() just prefixes cwd. For security checks (is this path inside the sandbox?), resolve first — then compare.
Glob with intent: p.glob('*.log') for one level, p.rglob('*.log') for recursive. rglob on huge trees is slow — scope it (start deep, filter early).
Temp files done right: tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) + os.replace for atomic writes. Never write directly to the final path — crashes leave half-files.

example.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('/var/log/app')
for f in p.rglob('*.log'):
    if f.is_file() and not f.is_symlink():  # skip symlinks: traversal safety
        process(f)
# atomic write:
tmp = Path('/var/lib/app/state.json.tmp')
tmp.write_text(json.dumps(state))
tmp.replace('/var/lib/app/state.json')  # atomic on POSIX
example.walkthrough: os.replace is atomic: readers see the old file or the new file, never a half-written one. The tmp+replace pattern is the filesystem's transaction — crashes leave the old version intact, not corruption. This is how databases write.

pitfalls: String-concatenated paths. os.sep bugs and injection via ..
Direct writes to final paths. Crash = corrupt file.
Following symlinks blindly in traversal. Symlink loops hang rglob forever.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one os.path-heavy function with pathlib; add the atomic-write pattern.

lessons.title: Traversal: Walking Trees Safely
concepts: os.walk vs rglob: walk gives control (topdown, prune dirs by editing dirnames), rglob gives brevity. For safety-critical traversal (deletion!), walk with pruning wins.
Symlink hazards: loops (a → b → a) hang naive recursion; escapes (.. through symlinks) break sandbox containment. Use os.scandir with follow_symlinks=False and track visited inodes.
Prune early: editing dirnames in topdown walk skips entire subtrees (skip .git, node_modules, __pycache__). Pruning is both a speedup and a safety boundary.
Count before acting: for destructive ops, first pass counts and lists, second pass acts — with the list logged. 'Delete what I found' without a manifest is how the wrong tree dies.

example.code:
import os
seen = set()
for root, dirs, files in os.walk('/data', topdown=True, followlinks=False):
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in ('.git', '__pycache__')]
    st = os.stat(root); seen.add((st.st_dev, st.st_ino))  # loop detection
    for f in files:
        process(os.path.join(root, f))
example.walkthrough: The dirs[:] slice assignment is the pruning mechanism: mutating the list in place tells walk not to descend. followlinks=False plus inode tracking closes the loop hazard. Together they make traversal safe on adversarial trees.

pitfalls: followlinks=True on untrusted trees. Loops and escapes.
Deleting during walk without a manifest. List first, act second.
No pruning. Walking .git wastes hours and risks hooks.
lessons.try_it: Write a safe disk-usage tool: walk with pruning, loop detection, and a summary.

lessons.title: Permissions and Ownership
concepts: Unix permissions: user/group/other × read/write/execute, in octal (0o755, 0o640). Know them cold — 0o777 is never the answer, and debugging 'permission denied' starts here.
umask shapes defaults: new files get 666 & ~umask. A umask of 0o022 gives 644 files; 0o077 gives 600. Set umask in daemons explicitly — inherited umasks are surprises.
Secrets need 0o600 (owner read/write only) and directories 0o700. Check on read: if the key file is world-readable, warn or refuse — fail safe on sloppy permissions.
Ownership in containers: files created as root are unreadable to the app user. chown in the Dockerfile or run as the right user from the start — permission bugs are the #1 'works locally' failure.

example.code:
import os, stat
KEY = Path('/etc/app/key.pem')
mode = stat.S_IMODE(KEY.stat().st_mode)
if mode & 0o077:
    raise SystemExit(f'refusing: {KEY} is group/world-accessible ({oct(mode)})')
# set explicitly when writing secrets:
KEY.write_bytes(secret)
KEY.chmod(0o600)
example.walkthrough: The check-on-read is defense in depth: even if deployment misconfigures, the app refuses to run with exposed secrets. Fail safe beats fail convenient — a crashed app is better than a leaked key.

pitfalls: 0o777 to 'fix' permissions. You fixed the symptom and created the vulnerability.
World-readable secrets. Check and refuse.
Root-owned files for app users. chown or run as the user.
lessons.try_it: Audit your project's secret files: permissions, ownership, and the check-on-read.

lessons.title: Atomicity and Durability
concepts: Atomic rename: os.replace gives all-or-nothing file updates. Readers never see partial writes — the foundation of crash-safe state files.

fsync for durability: write() lands in the OS page cache, not on disk. For state that must survive power loss, f.flush() + os.fsync(f.fileno()) before rename. Databases do this; your state file should too.
Directory fsync: after creating/renaming files, fsync the DIRECTORY fd — otherwise the rename itself may not survive a crash. The forgotten fsync.
Write-ahead pattern: write new state to tmp, fsync, rename over old, fsync dir. Crash at any point leaves old or new — never corrupt. This is SQLite's playbook in 10 lines.

example.code:
import os, json
def save_state(path, state):
    tmp = path + '.tmp'
    with open(tmp, 'w') as f:
        json.dump(state, f)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())
    os.replace(tmp, path)
    dfd = os.open(os.path.dirname(path) or '.', os.O_DIRECTORY)
    try:
        os.fsync(dfd)   # the forgotten fsync: persist the rename
    finally:
        os.close(dfd)
example.walkthrough: The directory fsync is what separates 'probably durable' from 'durable': without it, a power loss can lose the rename itself, leaving the tmp file and the old state. Each layer (file data, file metadata, directory entry) needs its own flush.

pitfalls: Assuming write() = on disk. Page cache is not persistence.
Skipping directory fsync. The rename can vanish on power loss.
Partial writes without tmp+replace. Crash mid-write = corrupt state.
lessons.try_it: Implement save_state with the full pattern; kill -9 mid-write 20x and verify integrity.

lessons.title: Watching Files: inotify and Polling
concepts: inotify (Linux) delivers filesystem events: no polling, instant notification, low CPU. watchdog abstracts it cross-platform — use the library, not raw inotify, unless you need the edge cases.
Event coalescing: rapid writes produce many events; editors produce atomic-save sequences (create tmp, rename). Debounce (act 500ms after last event) or you process half-written files.
Watch limits: inotify watches consume kernel resources (max_user_watches). Watching huge trees needs recursive watch setup and limit tuning — or a polling fallback for the long tail.
The atomic-save dance: many editors write tmp+rename, which looks like DELETE+CREATE, not MODIFY. Handle all three; test with vim, VS Code, and echo.

example.walkthrough: Debouncing separates event receipt from action: the handler records timestamps, a sweeper acts on quiescent paths. This absorbs the editor's tmp+rename dance and rapid-write bursts — process settled files, not events.

pitfalls: Acting on every event. Half-written files and editor tempfiles.
Polling huge trees at 1s. CPU burn; use inotify.
Ignoring DELETE+CREATE. Atomic saves don't look like modifies.
lessons.try_it: Build a debounced watcher; test with vim saves and rapid echo appends.

lessons.title: Sockets: The Fundamentals
concepts: A socket is an endpoint: socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) for TCP, SOCK_DGRAM for UDP. bind/listen/accept (server), connect (client) — the five-call dance that underlies everything.

TCP gives ordered, reliable byte streams; UDP gives unordered, unreliable datagrams. TCP for correctness (APIs, files), UDP for timeliness (DNS, gaming, streaming) — the trade is reliability vs latency.

Blocking vs non-blocking: blocking sockets stall the thread on recv; non-blocking raises BlockingIOError. Selectors (select/epoll) multiplex many sockets on one thread — the pre-asyncio pattern asyncio still uses.
Byte discipline: sockets move bytes, not messages. TCP has no message boundaries — you must frame (length prefix, delimiter, or fixed size). Assuming one send = one recv is the #1 socket bug.

example.code:
import socket
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(('127.0.0.1', 9000)); srv.listen(5)
conn, addr = srv.accept()
data = conn.recv(4096)  # bytes! may be partial — loop until framed
conn.sendall(data)      # sendall, not send: loops internally
example.walkthrough: SO_REUSEADDR avoids the 'address in use' purgatory after restarts (TIME_WAIT sockets). sendall vs send is the correctness detail: send may write partially, and partial writes without a loop lose data silently.

pitfalls: Assuming message boundaries on TCP. Frame explicitly.
send() without checking the return. Partial writes lose data.
Forgetting SO_REUSEADDR. Restarts fail on TIME_WAIT.
lessons.try_it: Write an echo server/client pair; then break message boundaries and fix with length-prefix framing.

lessons.title: TCP in Practice: Timeouts and Retries
concepts: Every network call needs a timeout: connect timeout, read timeout, total deadline. A socket without timeouts is a hang waiting for a network partition.
Retries need policy: retry idempotent operations (GETs), not non-idempotent ones (POSTs that charge) — or make operations idempotent (idempotency keys). Blind retries amplify outages.
Backoff with jitter, again: thundering herds retry simultaneously; jitter spreads them. Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency entirely — fail fast instead of queueing behind a corpse.
Half-open connections: the peer died silently (no FIN). TCP keepalives or application heartbeats detect them; without, you wait for the read timeout. Design for silent death.

example.code:
import socket
s = socket.create_connection(('api.example.com', 443), timeout=5)
s.settimeout(10)  # read/write timeout after connect
# retry policy sketch: 3 attempts, exponential backoff + jitter,
# only for idempotent ops; circuit-break after 5 consecutive failures
# half-open detection: SO_KEEPALIVE or app-level ping every 30s
example.walkthrough: The timeout layers compose: connect (5s), read (10s), total deadline (30s). Each bounds a different hang. The idempotency rule decides what may retry — charging twice is worse than failing once.

pitfalls: No timeouts. Partitions turn threads into monuments.
Retrying non-idempotent ops. Double-charges are worse than errors.
No jitter. Retry storms are self-inflicted DDoS.
lessons.try_it: Add timeouts + jittered retry to an HTTP client; test against a blackhole (iptables DROP).

lessons.title: HTTP Clients Done Right
concepts: Use a session (requests.Session / httpx.Client): connection pooling reuses TCP+TLS handshakes — creating a session per request is a performance bug and a port-exhaustion bug.
Timeouts as tuples: (connect, read) — never a bare number or none. httpx timeout=httpx.Timeout(5.0, read=10.0). The default (no timeout) is the bug.
Handle the status codes: raise_for_status() or explicit branches; 429 means back off (respect Retry-After); 5xx means maybe-retry; connection errors mean the network, not the API.
Streaming for large bodies: stream=True / httpx.stream() — don't load the 2GB response into RAM. And always close the response (context managers) or connections leak.

example.code:
import httpx
limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=50, max_keepalive_connections=20)
with httpx.Client(timeout=httpx.Timeout(5.0, read=30.0),
                  limits=limits) as c:
    r = c.get('https://api.example.com/items', params={'page': 2})
    r.raise_for_status()
    for item in r.json():
        process(item)  # small body; for large: httpx.stream
example.walkthrough: The session's pool is the performance: 50 connections reused across requests vs a TLS handshake per request. Limits bound resource use; timeouts bound hangs; the context manager guarantees cleanup. Four lines, four protections.

pitfalls: New session per request. Handshake per call; ephemeral-port exhaustion.
No timeouts. The default hangs forever.
Unclosed responses. Connection leaks under load.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark session-per-request vs shared session: measure handshake overhead.

lessons.title: Servers: From Socket to Framework
concepts: The server spectrum: raw sockets (learning) → http.server (toys) → WSGI (sync frameworks) → ASGI (async) → production servers (gunicorn/uvicorn with workers). Each layer trades control for convenience.
Concurrency model per server: threads (gunicorn sync workers), processes (prefork), asyncio (uvicorn). Match to workload: I/O-bound → async/threads; CPU-bound → processes. The GIL decides, again.

Production shape: reverse proxy (nginx) in front — TLS termination, static files, slow-client buffering — app server behind it. Never expose the app server directly; the proxy absorbs the internet's rudeness.
Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM → stop accepting, drain in-flight requests, then exit. Dropped connections on deploy are a server bug, not a deploy cost.

example.code:
# gunicorn: prefork, 2-4 workers per core for sync workloads
# gunicorn app:module --workers 4 --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker
# uvicorn: single-process asyncio; run N copies behind nginx
# graceful: gunicorn handles SIGTERM by draining workers (graceful_timeout)
# health: /health endpoint for the proxy/load balancer to check
example.walkthrough: The proxy+app split is separation of concerns: nginx handles TLS, buffering, and static files (its strengths); the app handles logic (its strength). Slow clients held by nginx never occupy app workers — the classic slowloris defense.

pitfalls: App server on the internet. No TLS termination, no buffering, no defense.
No graceful shutdown. Deploys drop in-flight requests.
Sync workers for I/O-bound APIs. Workers block on waits; async wouldn't.
lessons.try_it: Put nginx in front of a toy app; verify slow-client protection and graceful drain.

lessons.title: TLS: What You Must Get Right
concepts: TLS in 2026: use the ssl module's defaults (PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT), verify_mode=CERT_REQUIRED, check_hostname=True. The defaults are secure; the bugs come from disabling them.

Certificate verification is the whole game: unverified TLS is encryption without authentication — active attackers intercept freely. ssl._create_unverified_context is never the answer (fix the CA bundle instead).
SNI, ALPN, and session resumption are negotiated automatically by the defaults. You need to know they exist for debugging (openssl s_client), not for configuration.
Private CAs: install the CA cert into the trust store (certifi/ system store), don't disable verification. Mutual TLS (client certs) for service-to-service in zero-trust setups.

example.code:
import ssl, socket
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()  # secure defaults: verify + hostname check
with socket.create_connection(('example.com', 443)) as s:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(s, server_hostname='example.com') as tls:
        print(tls.version(), tls.getpeercert()['subject'])
# NEVER: ssl._create_unverified_context() — that's plaintext with extra steps
example.walkthrough: create_default_context is the secure-by-default API: verification and hostname checking on, modern TLS versions, safe ciphers. Every TLS bug in Python code comes from someone turning these off 'temporarily.'

pitfalls: Disabling verification 'temporarily.' Temporary becomes permanent; attackers don't care.
Ignoring cert expiry. Monitor it; automate renewal.
TLS without hostname check. Wrong-host certs accepted silently.
lessons.try_it: Connect to three sites with verification on; then diagnose an expired-cert site with openssl s_client.

lessons.title: Threads: When and How
concepts: Threads share memory: great for I/O-bound work (each thread waits independently), dangerous for shared state (races). The GIL means threads don't parallelize CPU work — they parallelize WAITING.
The pattern: ThreadPoolExecutor for task farms (fetch 100 URLs), with max_workers tuned (I/O-bound: dozens; CPU-bound: don't). Futures give results and exceptions cleanly.
Shared state needs discipline: locks for mutation, queues for communication. Prefer queues (share-nothing messaging) over locks (shared-everything) — queues make the handoff explicit.
Daemon threads die with the main program — use for background helpers, never for work that must complete. Join what matters; daemonize what doesn't.

example.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import httpx
urls = [...]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20) as ex:
    # I/O-bound: 20 threads overlap 20 waits
    results = list(ex.map(fetch_one, urls))
# exceptions propagate from .map; the with-block joins everything
example.walkthrough: ThreadPoolExecutor is the sane threads API: no manual start/join, exceptions surface, the context manager waits. max_workers=20 for I/O is a starting point — tune by measuring, not by core count (cores don't matter for waits).

pitfalls: Threads for CPU-bound work. The GIL serializes; use processes.
Unbounded thread creation. 10k threads = 10k stacks = OOM.
Shared mutable state without locks. Races are Heisenbugs — test won't catch them reliably.
lessons.try_it: Fetch 50 URLs with 1 vs 20 threads; measure the wall-clock difference.

lessons.title: Multiprocessing: Real Parallelism
concepts: Processes have separate memory and separate GILs: true parallelism for CPU-bound work. The cost: pickling data across the boundary, slower startup, harder debugging.
ProcessPoolExecutor mirrors the thread API — same map/submit shape, different physics. Chunksize matters: too small = pickling overhead dominates; too large = stragglers.
Shared state across processes needs explicit mechanisms: Queue/Pipe for messages, shared memory (Value/Array) for counters, Manager for convenience (slow). Default to message-passing.
The fork start method copies memory (fast, Unix); spawn is clean but slow (re-imports). Beware fork + threads (deadlocks) — and always guard with if __name__ == '__main__'.

example.code:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
def heavy(chunk):
    return sum(x*x for x in chunk)  # CPU-bound: GIL would serialize threads
if __name__ == '__main__':
    chunks = [range(i*10**6, (i+1)*10**6) for i in range(8)]
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
        total = sum(ex.map(heavy, chunks))  # real parallelism
example.walkthrough: The __main__ guard is mandatory with spawn (Windows/macOS default): without it, each child re-imports the module and spawns grandchildren recursively — the fork bomb you write yourself.

pitfalls: Forgetting __main__ guard. Recursive process spawning.
Tiny chunks. Pickle overhead eats the parallelism.
Sharing via globals. Processes don't share memory — pass messages.
lessons.try_it: Parallelize a CPU-bound loop with processes; tune chunksize and measure scaling.

lessons.title: asyncio: One Thread, Many Waits
concepts: asyncio runs coroutines on a single thread: await yields control during I/O waits, the event loop runs other coroutines. Thousands of connections, one thread — no GIL contention, no thread overhead.
The rules: async def for coroutines, await for waiting, never block the loop (no time.sleep, no requests — use asyncio.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient). One blocking call stalls everything.
Structured concurrency: asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) scopes task lifetimes — tasks can't outlive the group, exceptions propagate. create_task + gather works but leaks on cancellation.
Bridges: run_in_executor for blocking code (thread pool escape hatch), asyncio.to_thread for simple cases. The loop stays non-blocking; the blocking work goes elsewhere.

example.code:
import asyncio, httpx
async def fetch(client, url):
    r = await client.get(url, timeout=10)  # yields during wait
    return r.status_code
async def main(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            for u in urls:
                tg.create_task(fetch(client, u))  # scoped: no leaks
asyncio.run(main(urls))
example.walkthrough: TaskGroup is the modern pattern: it waits for all tasks, propagates the first exception, and cancels the rest — structured like a with-block. The old gather pattern left cancelled tasks dangling; TaskGroup doesn't.

pitfalls: Blocking the event loop. One time.sleep(10) freezes 10k connections.
Unbounded task creation. 100k tasks = memory blowout; use semaphores.
fire-and-forget create_task. Cancelled tasks vanish silently.
lessons.try_it: Fetch 200 URLs with asyncio + TaskGroup; compare with the threaded version.

lessons.title: Queues: The Communication Backbone
concepts: Queues decouple producers from consumers: put() never blocks the producer (until full), get() feeds workers. The bounded queue + N workers is the universal concurrency shape.
Bounded queues are backpressure: maxsize=N, put blocks when full — the producer slows instead of memory exploding. Unbounded queues are OOM with extra steps.
Shutdown protocol: sentinel values (None) per consumer, or task_done()/join() for completion tracking. Every queue needs a documented shutdown — orphaned consumers hang joins forever.
Choose the queue for the domain: queue.Queue (threads), multiprocessing.Queue (processes), asyncio.Queue (coroutines). Cross-domain needs bridges — don't mix them.

example.code:
import queue, threading
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=100)  # bounded: backpressure built in
def worker():
    while (item := q.get()) is not None:  # None = shutdown sentinel
        process(item)
        q.task_done()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
for item in source: q.put(item)       # blocks when full: backpressure
for _ in threads: q.put(None)        # one sentinel per consumer
q.join()                             # wait for all task_done()
example.walkthrough: The sentinel-per-consumer plus task_done/join is the complete lifecycle: production, consumption, shutdown, and completion — all explicit. Every missing piece is a hang: no sentinel → consumers never exit; no task_done → join never returns.

pitfalls: Unbounded queues. Memory grows with the producer-consumer gap.
No shutdown protocol. Joins hang; threads leak.
Mixing queue types across domains. Thread queue in async code deadlocks.
lessons.try_it: Build a producer/consumer pipeline with bounded queue; test shutdown and backpressure.

lessons.title: Locks, Races, and Deadlocks
concepts: Races: two threads mutate shared state; the outcome depends on scheduling. The fix hierarchy: avoid sharing (queues) > immutable data > locks (last resort). Less sharing, fewer races.
Locks done right: one lock per invariant, hold briefly, never call unknown code while holding (it might acquire another lock — deadlock). with lock: is the only shape; manual acquire/release leaks.

Deadlock's four conditions (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one: lock ordering (global order, always acquire in order) breaks circular wait — the practical fix.
Prefer higher-level tools: concurrent collections, atomic operations, and message-passing over raw locks. Every lock is a future deadlock; the best lock is the one you didn't need.

example.code:
import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
count = 0
def inc():
    global count
    with lock:          # brief, no calls inside that could lock
        count += 1
# lock ordering for two locks: ALWAYS acquire in the same global order
# with lock_a: with lock_b: ...   (never the reverse anywhere)
example.walkthrough: The with-statement is the discipline: acquisition and release are paired lexically, exceptions can't leak the lock. Lock ordering (a global acquisition order, documented) is the deadlock vaccine — circular wait becomes impossible.

pitfalls: Locking around I/O or callbacks. Unknown code + held lock = deadlock.
Inconsistent lock order. A→B here, B→A there: deadlock eventually.
Fine-grained locking everywhere. Complexity breeds the bugs it was meant to fix.
lessons.try_it: Write a two-lock program; demonstrate the deadlock, then fix with ordering.

lessons.title: Structured Logging
concepts: Log structured data (JSON), not prose: {'event': 'db_query', 'duration_ms': 42, 'rows': 7} is queryable; 'query took a while' is not. Structure is what makes logs searchable at scale.

The logging module done right: getLogger(__name__) per module, handlers configured once at startup (dictConfig), levels used honestly (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL). Root-logger basicConfig in libraries is a sin.
Context via correlation IDs: bind request_id at the edge, include it in every log. Without it, debugging a distributed request is archaeology across services.

Log at the right level and volume: INFO for business events, DEBUG for developer detail (off in prod), WARNING for 'wrong but handled', ERROR for 'failed, human may care'. Noisy logs hide the signal — and cost money.

example.walkthrough: The ctx dict is the correlation mechanism: whatever context you bind (request_id, user_id) rides on every record automatically. Querying 'all logs for request X' becomes a filter, not a forensic expedition.

pitfalls: f-strings as the log message with no structure. Unqueryable.
Logging in libraries with basicConfig. Config belongs to the app, not the lib.
DEBUG in production. Volume drowns signal; cost explodes.
lessons.try_it: Convert one module's print() debugging to structured logging with request IDs.

lessons.title: Metrics with prometheus_client
concepts: The four metric types: Counter (only up: requests, errors), Gauge (up/down: queue depth, temp), Histogram (distributions: latency — use for SLOs), Summary (client-side quantiles — avoid).
Label discipline: few, bounded-cardinality labels (method, status) — never user IDs or request IDs (cardinality explosion kills Prometheus). Labels are dimensions, not identifiers.
RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). RED answers 'is it working?'; USE answers 'why is the box sad?'
Expose /metrics, let Prometheus scrape. Push vs pull: pull (scrape) is the default — the monitor discovers targets; push (Pushgateway) only for batch jobs that die before scraping.

example.code:
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server
REQS = Counter('http_requests_total', 'requests', ['method', 'status'])
LAT = Histogram('http_request_seconds', 'latency', ['route'],
                buckets=(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5))
start_http_server(8000)  # /metrics for Prometheus
# in handler: REQS.labels('GET', '200').inc(); LAT.labels('/api').observe(d)
example.walkthrough: Histogram buckets are the SLO machinery: the p99 comes from buckets, so choose them around your SLO thresholds (0.5s SLO → buckets bracketing 0.5). Default buckets suit nobody; tune them to your objectives.

pitfalls: High-cardinality labels. user_id as a label = Prometheus OOM.
Averages from Summaries. Histograms give real quantiles.
No /metrics endpoint. Unscraped metrics don't exist.
lessons.try_it: Instrument a toy service with RED metrics; query rate/errors/p99 in Prometheus.

lessons.title: Health Checks and Readiness
concepts: Liveness vs readiness, again: liveness = 'restart me if dead' (cheap, local); readiness = 'send me traffic if able' (may check dependencies). Conflating them restarts what should merely shed load.
Health endpoints: /health/live (process alive), /health/ready (dependencies reachable). Keep checks fast and shallow — a health check that times out is worse than none.
Dependency checks with care: readiness failing when the DB is down removes the pod from service (good); liveness failing on DB outage restarts the pod pointlessly (bad — restarts don't fix the DB).
Startup probes for slow starters: models loading, caches warming — startupProbe guards the liveness probe during init. Without it, slow starters get killed before they're ready.

example.walkthrough: The split is the design: /live never depends on anything external (it answers 'is the process stuck?'), /ready may check dependencies (it answers 'should I get traffic?'). One endpoint doing both jobs does neither correctly.

pitfalls: Liveness checking dependencies. DB outage → restart storm.
Slow health checks. Timeouts cascade into false negatives.
No startup probe. Slow starters killed in a loop.
lessons.try_it: Add /live and /ready to a service; test each failure mode's behavior.

lessons.title: Alerting on Python Services
concepts: Alert on symptoms (error rate, latency SLO burn), not causes (CPU, memory) — the SRE rule, applied to your service. Pages mean user impact or budget burn.
Instrument the alertable: the metrics you need (RED + saturation) must exist before the alert. 'We can't alert on that' is an instrumentation gap, not an alerting gap.
Runbook per alert: symptom → diagnosis commands → fix → escalation. The alert fires at 3 AM; the runbook is the on-call's brain. No runbook, no alert.
Test alerts like code: fire them in staging (chaos the dependency, watch the page). Untested alerts are wishes — the first real fire is a bad time to learn the alert is misconfigured.

example.code:
Alert checklist:
  [ ] symptom-based (SLO burn or user-facing)
  [ ] metrics exist and are scraped (no gaps)
  [ ] runbook linked with first action
  [ ] tested in staging (fired on purpose)
  [ ] tuned: no false pages in 30 days
  An alert failing any check is a ticket, not a page.
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the quality gate: alerts are production code with a human in the loop. 'Tested in staging' is the most-skipped item and the most valuable — it verifies the whole chain (metric → rule → page → human → runbook).

pitfalls: Paging on CPU. Symptoms page; causes ticket.
Alerts without runbooks. 3 AM improvisation.
Untested alerts. The chain breaks at the worst moment.
lessons.try_it: Write one burn-rate alert for your service with runbook and staging test.

lessons.title: Tracing and Correlation
concepts: Tracing follows requests across services: spans (timed operations) with trace IDs propagated in headers. The waterfall shows where distributed latency lives.
Propagate context: the trace/span IDs ride HTTP headers (W3C traceparent), log records, and queue messages. Broken propagation = broken traces — instrument the edges (ingress, clients).
Sample wisely: head-based sampling (decide at ingress, e.g., 1%) keeps traces complete; tail-based keeps the interesting ones (errors, slow) but needs a collector. Errors: always sample.
Correlate the pillars: trace ID in logs, exemplar (trace ID) on metrics. One incident, one ID across metrics/traces/logs — the investigation flows without re-finding context.

example.code:
# W3C traceparent propagation (manual sketch):
# ingress: trace_id = random128(); span_id = random64()
# outbound: headers['traceparent'] = f'00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01'
# logs: include trace_id in every record's ctx
# metrics: exemplar={'trace_id': trace_id} on the histogram observe
# result: metric spike -> trace waterfall -> logs, one ID
example.walkthrough: The trace ID is the join key across pillars: it turns three separate investigations into one. Propagation is the hard part — every hop (HTTP, queue, subprocess) must forward it, or the trace fragments.

pitfalls: No propagation. Traces fragment at the first uninstrumented hop.
