100% sampling in prod. Cost and overhead explode; sample.
Trace IDs not in logs. The join key exists but nobody uses it.
lessons.try_it: Propagate a trace ID through two services into logs; verify the join.

lessons.title: argparse to Click: Choosing the Framework
concepts: argparse (stdlib): no dependencies, full control, verbose. Fine for simple tools; the boilerplate grows with subcommands.
Click/Typer: decorators/annotations define the interface — less boilerplate, better help, shell completion. Typer's type hints are self-documenting. The dependency is worth it past ~3 subcommands.
The interface contract: every command has --help that fully documents it, --version, and machine-readable output modes (--json/--format). Undocumented flags don't exist.
Exit codes as API: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 usage error, custom codes documented. Scripts compose via exit codes — yours should be meaningful.

example.walkthrough: Typer turns annotations into the interface: types validate, help generates, completion works. The docstring becomes the help text — documentation that can't rot because it's the code.

pitfalls: No --help. Undocumented CLIs are unusable CLIs.
Exit code always 0. Composition via exit codes requires honesty.
Positional args for everything. Flags are self-documenting; positions aren't.
lessons.try_it: Rebuild one script's argparse with Typer; compare line count and --help quality.

lessons.title: CLI UX: The Human Interface
concepts: Help-first design: write --help before the implementation. If the help is confusing, the interface is wrong — fix the interface, not the docs.
Sensible defaults, explicit overrides: the common case needs zero flags; every default documented. Configuration via flags > env > config file > defaults (explicit beats implicit).
Progress and feedback: long operations show progress (tqdm/rich), not silence. Silence breeds Ctrl-C. Errors go to stderr, results to stdout — pipes depend on it.
Idempotent, dry-run, and quiet modes: --dry-run shows what would happen (the safety), --quiet for scripts (parseable), --verbose for debugging. The three modes make the tool composable.

example.code:
import sys, typer
from rich.progress import track
@app.command()
def migrate(dry_run: bool = False, quiet: bool = False):
    plan = build_plan()
    if dry_run:
        for step in plan: print(f'would: {step}')  # stdout: the plan
        return
    for step in track(plan, description='migrating...'):  # stderr: progress
        step.run()
    if not quiet: print('done')  # hmm: results to stdout, chat to stderr
example.walkthrough: The stdout/stderr split is the composability contract: results on stdout (pipeable), human chatter on stderr. Breaking it breaks every pipeline your tool participates in. rich writes progress to stderr by default — correct.

pitfalls: Results on stderr. Pipes break.
Silent long operations. Users Ctrl-C what they can't see.
No --dry-run for destructive ops. Trust without verification.
lessons.try_it: Add --dry-run/--quiet/--verbose to a tool; verify stdout stays pipeable.

lessons.title: Output Design: Humans and Machines
concepts: Two audiences: humans (tables, colors, progress) and machines (--json, --format csv). Design both; default to human, offer machine. Parsing human output is the consumer's bug and your API failure.
Stable machine output: --json with a versioned schema. Humans tolerate layout changes; scripts don't. Version the schema; never break it silently.
Errors as data: non-zero exit + structured error to stderr (code, message, hint). 'Error: 1' is not an error message — say what failed and what to try.
Paging and truncation: long output respects --no-pager, truncates sanely, and never dumps 10k lines unexpectedly. Less is a feature.

example.walkthrough: The single-source-of-truth dict is the design: one data model, two renderers. Adding a format never touches the logic. The version field is the compatibility promise — bump it when the shape changes.

pitfalls: Only human output. Consumers parse your tables; then you redesign and break them.
Unversioned JSON. Schema changes break consumers silently.
Errors without hints. 'Failed' × exit 1 = support ticket.
lessons.try_it: Add --format json with a versioned schema to a tool; write a consumer script.

lessons.title: Configuration Precedence Done Right
concepts: The precedence chain: CLI flags > environment variables > config file > defaults. Explicit beats implicit; closer to the invocation wins. Document the chain — users will ask.
Validate at startup: schema-check the merged config, fail fast with the exact key and the fix. 'Failed at 3 AM on a typo' is a validation bug.
Secrets via env/files, never flags: --password on the command line lands in shell history and ps output. Env vars or secret files with tight permissions.
Config file formats: TOML for humans (typed, commented), YAML for the ecosystem (careful: Norway problem, use safe loaders), JSON for machines. Pick by audience.

example.walkthrough: The merge order IS the precedence: dict unpacking left-to-right, later wins. Validation after merging means one check covers all sources — and the error names the winning source, so users know what to fix.

pitfalls: Flags for secrets. ps aux shows them to everyone.
No validation. Typos surface at 3 AM.
Undocumented precedence. Users guess; guesses are wrong.
lessons.try_it: Implement the precedence chain for a tool; test each layer overriding the last.

lessons.title: Distribution: From Script to Tool
concepts: pyproject [project.scripts]: pip install gives a real command. The entry point is what turns 'clone and run' into 'install and use.'
Single binaries (PyInstaller/Nuitka/zipapp): for machines without Python or with hostile environments. zipapp for pure-Python (stdlib only!); PyInstaller for the kitchen sink.
Containers for services, binaries for agents: the log shipper that must run on 500 hosts wants a static binary, not a pip install dance. Match the artifact to the fleet.
Versioning and updates: --version honest, changelog maintained, update mechanism (or documented manual). A tool without updates rots; a tool with silent updates surprises.

example.code:
[project.scripts]
logship = 'logship.cli:main'   # pip install -> `logship` command
# zipapp: python -m zipapp app/ -p '/usr/bin/env python3' -o logship.pyz
# pyinstaller: pyinstaller --onefile --name logship cli.py
# pick: zipapp (pure stdlib) < pyinstaller (deps) < container (services)
example.walkthrough: The artifact ladder matches deployment reality: zipapp for stdlib-only tools (tiny, transparent), PyInstaller for dependency-heavy agents (self-contained), containers for services (full environment). Each rung trades size for completeness.

pitfalls: 'Clone the repo' as installation. Not a tool.
No --version. Unidentifiable binaries in production.
Silent auto-updates. Surprise restarts at 3 AM.
lessons.try_it: Distribute a tool two ways (pip entry point + zipapp); install both fresh.

lessons.title: Twelve-Factor Config
concepts: Config varies between deploys; code doesn't: the twelve-factor rule. Config = everything that varies (endpoints, credentials, feature flags, timeouts) — it lives in the environment, not the repo.
Strict separation: code (versioned, same everywhere) vs config (per-environment, never in git — especially secrets). 'It works in dev' failures are usually config leaks into code.
Granularity: one app, one config schema. Shared config files across services couple their deploys — the 'common config' that changes for service A breaks service B.
Config as code-adjacent: the schema is versioned with the app; the values live per-environment. Schema changes are deploys; value changes are operations.

example.code:
The separation test:
  Could you open-source the repo right now?
  If secrets/URLs would leak -> they're in code, not config.
  If the app can't start without env-specific files -> config isn't
  cleanly separated.
  The test is brutal and clarifying.
example.walkthrough: The open-source test makes the boundary visceral: anything you'd have to scrub is config masquerading as code. It's the fastest audit for config hygiene.

pitfalls: Secrets in git. History never forgets; scanners never sleep.
Env-specific code branches. if ENV == 'prod': is config in code.
Shared config blobs. Coupling via configuration.
lessons.try_it: Run the open-source test on a repo; list everything that would leak.

lessons.title: Validation: Fail Fast at Startup
concepts: Validate the entire config at startup: schema (types, ranges, required keys), cross-field rules (if tls then cert_path), and connectivity (can we reach the DB?). Fail in seconds, not at 3 AM.
Error messages as UX: name the key, show the bad value, say what's expected, suggest the fix. 'Invalid config' is not an error message — it's a riddle.
Use a schema library (pydantic/dataclasses + validation): typed models with validators beat hand-rolled dict checks. The schema IS the documentation.
Distinguish fatal vs degradable: missing DB endpoint = fatal (can't work); missing metrics endpoint = warn and continue (degraded). Not every bad key deserves a crash.

example.walkthrough: Pydantic's error messages do the UX work: they name the field, show the value, state the constraint. The model is simultaneously the schema, the validator, and the documentation — one source of truth.

pitfalls: Hand-rolled dict validation. Inconsistent errors, missed keys.
'Invalid config' messages. Riddles, not errors.
Validating lazily. First use at 3 AM instead of startup.
lessons.try_it: Add pydantic validation to a tool; feed it 5 bad configs and read the errors.

lessons.title: Secrets in Configuration
concepts: Secrets are config with extra rules: never in git, never in logs, rotated regularly, least-privilege access. The config system must treat them as a separate class, not just 'another key.'

Delivery patterns: env vars (simple, visible in /proc), files (0o600, mounted by orchestrators), secret managers (Vault/cloud — rotation + audit). Match to threat model: files beat env for shared hosts.
Reference, don't embed: config holds the secret's NAME/path (vault: prod/db/password), the app resolves at startup. The config file stays committable; the values never touch disk unencrypted.
Rotation support: the app must handle secret change without restart (reload on signal/file watch) or accept rolling restarts. Unrotatable secrets don't rotate — design for it.

example.code:
Secret config shape:
  # config.toml (committable):
  [database]
  password_ref = 'vault://prod/db/password'  # reference, not value
  # app startup: resolve refs -> values (memory only)
  # rotation: SIGHUP re-resolves; or file-watch on the secret file
  The config never contains the secret. The git history never sees it.
example.walkthrough: The reference pattern keeps config committable and auditable while values stay in the manager. Rotation becomes 'update the manager + signal the app' — no config change, no deploy, no git history pollution.

pitfalls: Secrets in config files in git. The #1 secret leak vector.
Env-var-only for shared hosts. /proc is world-readable.
No rotation path. Static secrets are compromised secrets (eventually).
lessons.try_it: Convert one embedded secret to the reference pattern; test rotation.

lessons.title: Feature Flags as Config
concepts: Flags decouple deploy from release: code ships dark, flags enable gradually. The flag system is config with a UI and audit trail — not an env var you SSH to change.
Flag hygiene: every flag has an owner, a creation date, and a removal ticket. Stale flags are tech debt with runtime behavior — the flag graveyard breaks things mysteriously.
Targeting and rollout: percentage rollouts, user cohorts, kill switches. The flag evaluation must be fast and local (no network per check) — flags are read millions of times.
Flags are not config for everything: infrastructure topology, credentials, and security boundaries don't belong in flags. Flags control behavior; config controls deployment.

example.code:
# flag discipline in code:
if flags.enabled('new-parser', user_id, default=False):
    parse_v2(line)
else:
    parse_v1(line)
# every flag: owner, ticket, expiry
# FLAGS.md: name | owner | created | remove-by | status
# CI check: flags older than 90 days fail the build (force cleanup)
example.walkthrough: The CI check is the hygiene enforcer: flags with expired remove-by dates break the build, forcing either removal or explicit extension. Without it, flags accumulate until nobody dares touch them.

pitfalls: Permanent flags. Every flag is tech debt until removed.
Flags for secrets/topology. Wrong tool; use config.
Network-per-check flags. Latency and failure mode in the hot path.
lessons.try_it: Inventory your flags; assign every one an owner and remove-by date.

lessons.title: Environment Discipline
concepts: Dev/stage/prod parity: same config SCHEMA everywhere, different values. Schema drift between environments ('prod has an extra key') is a deployment bug class.
Local dev: .env files for convenience, .env.example committed as the schema documentation. Never commit .env — the example is the contract, the file is personal.
Config diffing: diff effective config between environments before promoting. 'What differs between stage and prod?' should be answerable in one command (--show-effective-config per env).
Immutable config per deploy: the config that ran is recorded (versioned, snapshotted). Debugging 'what was prod running Tuesday?' needs the answer — not the current file.

example.code:
# .env.example: the schema contract (committed)
APP_ENDPOINT=https://api.example.com
APP_TIMEOUT=30
# .env: personal values (gitignored)
# promote check: diff effective configs
# diff <(app --show-config --env stage) <(app --show-config --env prod)
example.walkthrough: The diff-before-promote is the change management: environment differences are expected (endpoints, secrets) but should be enumerated, not surprising. Unexpected diffs are the bugs — catch them before prod does.

pitfalls: .env committed. Secrets in git, again.
Schema drift between envs. 'Works on stage' means nothing.
No config history. Tuesday's prod config is unknowable.
lessons.try_it: Add --show-effective-config; diff stage vs prod and explain every line.

lessons.title: Measure First: The Profiling Discipline
concepts: Profile before optimizing: 90% of 'slow' guesses are wrong about the bottleneck. cProfile for 30 seconds beats a week of rewriting the wrong function.
The method: reproduce with a benchmark script, measure (profile), hypothesize ONE change, measure again. One variable at a time — two changes and you don't know what helped.
Wall-clock vs CPU: time.perf_counter for elapsed, cProfile for CPU breakdown. I/O-bound slowness needs different tools (py-spy, async debug) than CPU-bound.
Define 'fast enough' first: the SLO (p99 < 500ms) decides when to stop. Optimization without a target is infinite — and the last 10% costs more than the first 90%.

example.code:
import cProfile, pstats, io
pr = cProfile.Profile()
pr.enable()
run_workload()          # the realistic benchmark, not a micro-test
pr.disable()
s = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=s).sort_stats('cumulative').print_stats(20)
print(s.getvalue())       # top 20 by cumulative time: start here
example.walkthrough: Cumulative time is the key sort: it shows where time is SPENT (including callees), not just where the clock ticks. The top of the cumulative list is the bottleneck — optimize there or nowhere.

pitfalls: Optimizing without profiling. Guessing the bottleneck.
Micro-benchmarks as proof. Realistic workloads or it didn't happen.
No stop condition. 'Faster' is not a requirement.
lessons.try_it: Profile a slow script; find the true bottleneck; verify your guess was wrong.

lessons.title: cProfile and Friends
concepts: cProfile: deterministic, function-level, stdlib. Sort by cumulative (where time goes) and tottime (where CPU burns, excluding callees). The two sorts answer different questions.
py-spy: sampling profiler for running processes — no code changes, no restart. py-spy top is htop for Python; flame graphs show the call tree visually.
line_profiler / scalene: line-level attribution when function-level isn't enough. 'Which line in this loop?' — line granularity for the hot function.
Yappi adds thread-awareness: per-thread CPU time. For threaded programs, cProfile's global view misleads — yappi shows which thread burns.

example.code:
python -m cProfile -o prof.out app.py        # deterministic
py-spy record -o flame.svg -- python app.py  # sampling, flame graph
py-spy top --pid <pid>                        # live, no restart
# read the flame: wide plateaus = hot code; wide = time share
example.walkthrough: Flame graphs read by width: the widest plateaus are where time goes. Click into them for the call path. Sampling (py-spy) has lower overhead than deterministic (cProfile) — use sampling in production, deterministic in dev.

pitfalls: cProfile in production. Overhead distorts; sample instead.
Sorting by ncalls. Called-often isn't slow; cumulative time is.
Ignoring the flame's width. Width IS the measurement.
lessons.try_it: Profile the same workload with cProfile and py-spy; compare the top functions.

lessons.title: Memory: Finding the Leak
concepts: tracemalloc: stdlib allocation tracking — where was this memory allocated? Start it early (it only tracks after start), compare snapshots to find growth.
The leak pattern: snapshot, run workload, snapshot, diff — growing allocations name the leak. Common culprits: unbounded caches, forgotten listeners, global lists.
__slots__: for millions of small objects, slots eliminate per-instance dicts (50%+ memory saved). The trade: no dynamic attributes — design for it upfront.
Generational GC: Python frees cycles automatically, but slowly. gc.get_objects() + objgraph for the stubborn ones. del doesn't free; refcount zero does.

example.code:
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
# ... run workload ...
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
# ... run workload again ...
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snap2.compare_to(snap1, 'lineno')[:10]:
    print(stat)  # growing allocations first: the leak suspects
example.walkthrough: The snapshot diff is the leak detector: stable allocations cancel out, growth surfaces. The lineno attribution points at the allocating line — which is usually a cache-append or listener-register away from where you'd look.

pitfalls: Guessing at leaks. tracemalloc diffs or it didn't happen.
Unbounded caches. Every cache needs a size policy (lru_cache(maxsize=)).
Ignoring __slots__ for hot objects. Dicts per instance add up at millions.
lessons.try_it: Leak a list deliberately; find it with tracemalloc diff in under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Algorithmic Wins: The Big Levers
concepts: Complexity first: O(n²) → O(n log n) beats micro-optimization by orders of magnitude. The profiler finds the hot function; complexity analysis finds the hot algorithm.
The usual suspects: list membership in loops (→ set), string concatenation in loops (→ join), repeated regex compilation (→ precompile), N+1 queries (→ batch). Each is a 10-100x win.
Vectorize with NumPy: Python loops over arrays → NumPy ops (C-speed, GIL released). The 100x lever for numeric code — and the reason 'Python is slow' is usually 'Python loops are slow.'
Cache deliberately: functools.lru_cache for pure functions, with maxsize and typed. Caching without invalidation is a correctness bug; caching without bounds is a memory leak.

example.code:
import re, functools
# before: O(n*m) membership in a loop
# for x in items: if x in big_list: ...        # O(n) per check!
# after:
big_set = set(big_list)                        # O(1) per check
# string building:
# out = ''
# for s in parts: out += s                     # O(n^2) copying!
out = ''.join(parts)                          # O(n) once
pat = re.compile(r'\d+')                     # precompile outside loops
example.walkthrough: Each fix is a complexity change disguised as a one-liner: set membership (O(n)→O(1)), join (O(n²)→O(n)), precompiled regex (amortized). The profiler points at the line; the complexity lens rewrites it.

pitfalls: Micro-optimizing the O(n²). Change the complexity, not the constants.
Unbounded lru_cache. Memory leak with a decorator.
Python loops over NumPy arrays. Use the vectorized ops.
lessons.try_it: Take a slow loop; apply set/join/precompile; measure each win separately.

lessons.title: Honest Optimization: Know the Limits
concepts: Amdahl's law: speedup is limited by the sequential fraction. Optimizing the 10% that parallelizes gives at most 1.1x — profile-guided effort goes to the dominant fraction.
The GIL ceiling: CPU-bound Python threads don't scale — multiprocessing, C extensions, or PyPy/numba for the hot loop. Know which ceiling you're hitting before building.
Trade-offs are real: readability, memory, latency, throughput — pick two loudly. The 'optimized' code nobody can maintain is a liability with benchmarks.
When to stop: SLO met + headroom = done. Every further optimization has negative ROI (complexity risk > speed gain). 'Fast enough' is an engineering decision, not a surrender.

example.code:
Amdahl check:
  hot function = 60% of runtime -> max speedup from it: 1/0.4 = 2.5x
  hot function = 10% of runtime -> max: 1/0.9 = 1.11x
  Effort goes to the 60%, never the 10%.
  And: is 2.5x needed? (SLO says p99 < 500ms; we're at 300ms -> STOP)
example.walkthrough: Amdahl's law is the prioritization tool: it converts 'this is slow' into 'this is worth X at most.' Combined with the SLO stop-condition, it prevents both under-optimization (missing the target) and over-optimization (gold-plating).

pitfalls: Optimizing the 10%. Amdahl says: don't.
Threads for CPU-bound. The GIL ceiling is real.
No stop condition. Infinite optimization, infinite risk.
lessons.try_it: Apply Amdahl to your last optimization: was the effort on the dominant fraction?

lessons.title: pytest: The Working Core
concepts: Test discovery and structure: test_*.py, test_* functions, plain asserts — pytest's assertion rewriting gives rich failure output from simple code. No boilerplate test classes needed.

Fixtures for setup: @pytest.fixture builds the resource (tmp dir, test DB, client), yields it, tears down. Scope (function/class/module/session) controls cost — session-scoped for the expensive stuff.
Parametrize for coverage: @pytest.mark.parametrize runs the same test over inputs — the table-driven pattern that turns 20 copy-paste tests into one.
Markers and selection: -m 'not slow', -x (stop at first failure), -k (name filter). The slow suite runs nightly; the fast suite gates every commit.

example.walkthrough: The fixture's yield is the setup/teardown contract: code before yield builds, after yield cleans — guaranteed even on test failure. Parametrize multiplies the test's value per line: one test, N cases, each reported separately.

pitfalls: Setup in the test body. Duplicated setup rots; fixtures don't.
No teardown. Test pollution (leaked state) causes order-dependent failures.
Copy-paste test variants. Parametrize them.
lessons.try_it: Convert three copy-paste tests to one parametrized test with a fixture.

lessons.title: Mocking: Boundaries, Not Everything
concepts: Mock at the boundary: external services, the filesystem, time, randomness — the things that are slow, flaky, or non-deterministic. Don't mock your own logic; test it.

unittest.mock essentials: Mock()/MagicMock() for fakes, patch() for replacement (as decorator or context manager), assert_called_with for verification. Patch where it's LOOKED UP, not where it's defined.
The patch-target rule: patch('mymodule.requests') if mymodule did 'import requests' — you patch the name in the user's namespace. Patching the definition site does nothing.
Don't mock what you can fake: a FakeDatabase (in-memory dict) beats a Mock for complex interactions — fakes have behavior, mocks have expectations. Over-mocking tests the mock, not the code.

example.walkthrough: The patch target is the #1 mocking bug: 'mymodule.requests' because mymodule bound the name requests. If mymodule did 'from requests import get', you'd patch 'mymodule.get'. The rule: patch the namespace that uses it.

pitfalls: Mocking your own code. Test the logic; mock the boundary.
Wrong patch target. Nothing happens; test passes vacuously.
Asserting nothing on the mock. Unverified mocks prove nothing.
lessons.try_it: Mock an HTTP boundary correctly; deliberately patch the wrong target and observe the vacuous pass.

lessons.title: Integration Tests: The Real Thing
concepts: Integration tests exercise real components: real SQLite/Postgres (testcontainers), real files, real subprocesses. They catch what unit tests can't — the seams.
Testcontainers pattern: spin the real dependency in Docker, run tests, tear down. Slower than mocks, truer than mocks — the middle ground that catches config and protocol bugs.
Subprocess testing: run the actual CLI (subprocess.run on the entry point), assert exit codes and outputs. The CLI is the product — test the product, not just the functions.
Mark and separate: @pytest.mark.integration, run in CI after unit tests (or nightly). Slow integration tests blocking every commit get skipped — schedule them where they'll actually run.

example.code:
import subprocess, pytest
@pytest.mark.integration
def test_cli_end_to_end(tmp_path):
    log = tmp_path / 'app.log'
    log.write_text('2024-01-01 ERROR boom\n')
    r = subprocess.run(['logship', 'scan', str(log)],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
    assert r.returncode == 0
    assert 'ERROR' in r.stdout  # the real binary, real file, real exit code
example.walkthrough: Testing the installed entry point (not the Python function) verifies packaging, console scripts, and arg parsing — the layers unit tests never touch. The tmp_path fixture keeps it hermetic.

pitfalls: Only unit tests. The seams are where systems break.
Integration tests in the fast suite. They'll be skipped; schedule them right.
Testing against shared dev databases. Flaky, coupled, dangerous.
lessons.try_it: Write one end-to-end CLI test via subprocess; run it in CI.

lessons.title: Fixtures and Test Design
concepts: Fixture composition: fixtures take other fixtures (db(client)) — build complex setups from simple pieces. conftest.py shares fixtures across files; keep them close to their tests.
Factories over fixtures for variation: a make_user(admin=True) factory beats 5 fixtures. Fixtures for the common case, factories for the variants.
Deterministic tests: fixed seeds (random.seed(42)), frozen time (freezegun), tmp dirs. Non-determinism in tests is flakiness waiting for CI to find it.
Test names as documentation: test_rejects_expired_token reads as a spec. When it fails, the name says what broke — future-you will thank present-you.

example.walkthrough: The factory-fixture hybrid is the scaling pattern: the fixture provides the builder, each test configures its variant. It avoids both fixture explosion (one per variant) and setup duplication (inline everywhere).

pitfalls: Fixtures for variants. Factories compose; fixtures multiply.
Random test data unseeded. Flaky by construction.
test_1, test_2 names. The failure message is useless.
lessons.try_it: Refactor a fixture-heavy test file: extract one factory, delete three fixtures.

lessons.title: Testing the Untestable: Time, Randomness, Concurrency
concepts: Time: freezegun freezes datetime; for asyncio, advance the loop manually. Never sleep in tests — inject the clock (a now() parameter) so tests control time.
Randomness: seed it (random.seed) or inject the RNG. Property-based testing (hypothesis) goes further: it FINDS the edge cases your examples missed — run it on parsers and serializers.

Concurrency: test the protocol, not the schedule — deterministic harnesses (single-threaded event loop, scripted interleavings) beat 'run 1000x and hope.' Stress tests find races; they don't prove absence.
The untestable remainder: some things (exact timing, real network partitions) are tested in staging/chaos, not unit tests. Know the boundary — don't contort unit tests into integration tests.

example.walkthrough: Property-based testing inverts the work: you state the invariant (never crashes, round-trips, idempotent), and hypothesis searches for violations. It finds the cases your imagination didn't — which is most of them.

pitfalls: sleep() in tests. Slow, flaky, and time-dependent.
Testing randomness without seeds. CI roulette.
'Ran 1000x green' as proof. Stress finds bugs; it doesn't certify.
lessons.try_it: Add one hypothesis property test to a parser; watch it find an edge case.

lessons.title: Live Coding: Systems Flavor
concepts: Systems live-coding differs from algorithms: expect 'write a rate limiter,' 'parse this log format,' 'implement a retry with backoff' — practical, library-aware, tested as you go.
The method: clarify (inputs? scale? failure modes?), sketch the interface, implement the happy path, then handle errors. Narrate trade-offs ('using a dict; for distributed I'd use Redis').
Use the stdlib confidently: collections, itertools, heapq, bisect — reaching for them signals fluency. Reimplementing Counter by hand signals the opposite.
Test as you go: run the snippet, show the edge case, fix it live. Interviewers trust code they've seen run more than code that's 'obviously right.'

example.walkthrough: The snippet's completeness is the signal: transient-only retries (not blind), jitter (thundering herds), loud failure (no silent swallowing). Three lines of policy in ten lines of code — that's systems fluency.

pitfalls: Silent pseudocode. Run it — or it's a sketch, not a solution.
No error handling. The happy path is half the problem.
Reaching for exotic libs. Stdlib first; explain the trade.
lessons.try_it: Practice: implement rate limiter, LRU cache, and retry — timed, narrated, tested.

lessons.title: Systems Design in Python Interviews
concepts: The Python systems design round: 'design a log shipper,' 'a task queue,' 'a config service' — they want components, data flow, failure modes, and the Python specifics (GIL? asyncio? multiprocessing?).

Structure: requirements (throughput? durability? latency?) → components (producers, queues, workers, storage) → Python mapping (which concurrency model per component, and why) → failure modes → monitoring.

Always name the Python constraints: 'CPU-bound workers → multiprocessing (GIL); 10k connections → asyncio; exactly-once → offset tracking + idempotent sinks.' The language-specific reasoning is what's graded.
End with operations: deploy, monitor, debug. 'How do you know it's broken? How do you fix it at 3 AM?' — the operability questions separate seniors.

example.code:
Design skeleton (log shipper):
  REQ: 50k lines/s, <5s latency, zero loss on restart
  COMP: tailer (inotify) -> bounded queue -> parsers (processes)
         -> batcher -> sink (idempotent HTTP)
  PYTHON: parsers = multiprocessing (CPU); tailer = thread+inotify;
          offsets in SQLite (atomic)
  FAIL: sink down -> bounded queue blocks (backpressure); kill -9 ->
        offsets resume; parse errors -> dead letter + metric
  OPS: /health, RED metrics, runbook for backpressure
example.walkthrough: Every line earns its place: the requirement justifies the component, the Python mapping names the constraint (GIL), the failure modes show operational thinking. Generic boxes don't pass; Python-specific reasoning does.

pitfalls: Language-agnostic boxes. They hired a Python engineer; show Python thinking.
No failure modes. 'What breaks?' is the senior question.
Skipping the requirements. Designing before knowing the scale.
lessons.try_it: Design a task queue in 40 minutes, recorded; review the Python-specific reasoning.

lessons.title: Debugging Scenarios: The Interview
concepts: The format: 'production is slow / leaking / deadlocking — walk me through your diagnosis.' They grade method: reproduce → measure → hypothesize → verify. Tool names matter less than the order.

The toolkit narrative: 'I'd check metrics first (what changed?), then py-spy (where's time going?), tracemalloc (if memory), faulthandler (if hung).' Naming the right tool per symptom shows experience.
Always state the hypothesis before the command: 'I suspect a pipe deadlock because the hang is size-dependent — let me check with...' Hypotheses first is what separates debugging from flailing.
Know the classics cold: pipe deadlock, GIL contention, connection leaks, fd exhaustion, thundering herd, cache stampede. Interviews recycle them because production recycles them.

example.code:
Debug narrative (slow service):
  1. SYMPTOM: p99 2s, was 200ms; when did it change? (metrics)
  2. HYPOTHESIS: downstream slowdown vs own regression
  3. TEST: traces — which span grew? (not guesses)
  4. FOUND: DB span 1.8s; check DB metrics (locks? slow query?)
  5. FIX: the missing index; verify p99 recovers
  Narrate the elimination; the method is the answer.
example.walkthrough: The narrative's discipline is elimination order: symptoms → localization → cause → fix → verify. Each step rules something out. Interviewers listen for the order — random tool-spraying fails even with the right tools.

pitfalls: Tool-spraying without hypotheses. Activity isn't diagnosis.
Skipping 'when did it change?' The timeline is the best diagnostic.
No verification. 'Fixed' without measuring is hoping.
lessons.try_it: Practice: take a real past incident; narrate the diagnosis in 5 minutes.

lessons.title: The Python Details Interviewers Probe
concepts: The GIL: what it is, when it matters (CPU-bound threads), the workarounds (multiprocessing, C extensions, free-threading). 'Threads for I/O, processes for CPU' — with the why.
Memory model: refcounting + GC, __slots__, tracemalloc, the GIL's cousin (memory never truly shared between processes). 'Why is my worker growing?' should have a 3-step answer.
Import system and packaging: sys.path, virtualenvs, entry points, the __main__ guard. 'It works on my machine' questions probe exactly this.
The stdlib map: subprocess, os, socket, asyncio, logging, argparse, pathlib, json, sqlite3 — know which module owns which problem. 'Which module would you reach for?' is the fluency test.

example.code:
Rapid-fire prep (answer in 30s each):
  - Thread vs process for 100 HTTP fetches? (threads/asyncio: I/O)
  - Counter shared across processes? (multiprocessing.Value/Queue)
  - Hang with no traceback? (faulthandler SIGUSR1 / py-spy)
  - Memory growing? (tracemalloc diff)
  - Subprocess hangs on big output? (communicate, not wait)
  - 10k connections? (asyncio, not threads)
  Speed + correctness = the interview signal.
example.walkthrough: The rapid-fire format trains the actual interview skill: instant, correct, with the reason attached. Each answer is a decision rule, not trivia — 'threads for I/O because the GIL only blocks compute.'

pitfalls: Trivia without reasons. 'Threads for I/O' needs the GIL explanation.
Guessing at tools. Name the right tool per symptom.
Slow, hedged answers. 30 seconds, committed, with the why.
lessons.try_it: Drill the rapid-fire list daily until each answer is instant with reasoning.

lessons.title: Your 6-Week Study Plan
concepts: Weeks 1-2: foundations — subprocess, filesystem, config. Labs daily; the bug ledger starts. Every lesson example runs in your terminal.
Weeks 3-4: the hard core — networking, concurrency, performance. This is where interviews live; break things deliberately (deadlocks, races, leaks).
Week 5: production — logging, CLI, testing. Build the capstone's phases 1-2 as you learn; the tool grows with the curriculum.
Week 6: integration — finish the capstone, mock twice, drill rapid-fire, rehearse the debug narratives. Performance, not new content.

example.code:
Weekly cadence:
  4x 90-min sessions (lesson -> run examples -> scenarios -> lab)
  1x bug-ledger review (every entry re-tested)
  1x capstone session (the tool grows weekly)
  Week 3: mock #1 (diagnostic) | Week 6: mock #2 (dress rehearsal)
  Daily: 15-min rapid-fire drill
example.walkthrough: The cadence front-loads the hard domains (weeks 3-4) so they get the most repetition. The capstone grows alongside — week 6 has a demo, not a cram session.

pitfalls: Cramming concurrency in week 6. The hard stuff needs the most reps.
Skipping the ledger review. Unrevisited misses are unlearned.
No mock until 'ready.' Measurement creates readiness.
lessons.try_it: Block the 6 weeks now; schedule mock #1 for week 3.

labs.title: Concurrent fetching with asyncio
labs.objective: Compare sequential vs concurrent fetching with asyncio and observe the wall-clock difference.
steps: Write /tmp/fsd-async/fetch.py that fetches a list of URLs twice: once awaiting each in a loop, once with asyncio.gather over create_task calls
Use httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp; add time.perf_counter() around each phase and print both durations
Run `python3 /tmp/fsd-async/fetch.py https://example.com https://example.org` (repeat the URLs ~20x via shell brace expansion)
Confirm the gather phase is dramatically faster while CPU stays low
Add a semaphore (asyncio.Semaphore(5)) variant and observe how it bounds concurrency
Note in one sentence when asyncio helps (I/O-bound) and when it does not (CPU-bound)

labs.title: Package a CLI with pyproject.toml
labs.objective: Turn a script into an installable package with a console entry point and install it into a venv.
steps: Create /tmp/fsd-pkg/src/greet/__init__.py and cli.py with a main() that prints a greeting via argparse
Write pyproject.toml with [project] (name, version, requires-python, dependencies) and [project.scripts] mapping greet = "greet.cli:main"
Add [build-system] requiring setuptools (or hatchling) as the PEP 517 backend
Create a fresh venv, then `pip install /tmp/fsd-pkg` and confirm the `greet` command is on PATH
Run `greet --name Ada` and confirm the output; run `pip show greet` to inspect the installed metadata
Bump the version in pyproject.toml, reinstall, and confirm pip show reflects it

Run the installed console script: greet --name Ada

labs.title: Deadlock Zoo
labs.objective: Reproduce the three classic subprocess deadlocks, then fix each.
steps: Deadlock 1: PIPE + wait() on large output — reproduce the hang (with timeout guard), then fix with communicate().
Deadlock 2: child waiting for stdin EOF while parent waits for child — fix by closing stdin.
Deadlock 3: two processes piped, both writing large outputs — fix by streaming/threading the reads.
For each: write the broken version (guarded), observe the hang, write the fixed version.
Document the rule each violates in your bug ledger.

checks.expect_contains: close what the child waits for

labs.title: Supervisor with Backoff
labs.objective: Build a process supervisor: restart with jittered backoff, crash cap, and health checks.
steps: Write a flaky worker (crashes randomly, sometimes hangs, sometimes poison-messages).
Write the supervisor: Popen, wait with timeout, jittered exponential backoff, crash cap with alert.
Add a health check (HTTP /health or heartbeat file); restart on failed checks, not just exits.
Test: poison message → dead-lettered, cap reached → alert, hang → killed and restarted.
Measure: time-to-recovery for each failure class; tune backoff parameters.

labs.title: Crash-Safe State File
labs.objective: Implement the full atomic+durable write pattern and prove it under kill -9.
steps: Implement save_state with tmp write, file fsync, os.replace, and directory fsync.
Write a loop: 1000 save/load cycles with random kill -9 of the writer mid-cycle.
After each kill, verify: state.json loads (old or new, never corrupt) and tmp files don't accumulate.
Remove the directory fsync; rerun — observe whether failures appear (they're rare; that's the point).
Document the pattern as your team's standard; note the fsync cost (measure it).

labs.title: Safe Tree Walker
labs.objective: Build a traversal tool with pruning, cycle detection, and a delete manifest.
steps: Write a walker: os.walk topdown, followlinks=False, prune (.git, __pycache__, node_modules), track (dev,ino) for cycles.
Add symlink-loop test fixtures (a/b -> a); verify the walker terminates and reports the loop.
Add a --delete mode with two passes: pass 1 builds and logs the manifest, pass 2 acts only on the manifest.
Test the sandbox check: resolve each path, verify it stays within the root, refuse otherwise.
Run against a large real tree; compare time with and without pruning.

labs.title: Framed Echo Service
labs.objective: Build a TCP echo server/client with length-prefix framing, then break and fix it.
steps: Write the naive version (no framing); demonstrate glued/split messages with rapid sends.
Add length-prefix framing (4-byte big-endian header); loop recv until complete.
Test: 10k messages, random sizes, verify echo integrity (hash each message).
Add timeouts (connect/read) and test against a blackhole server (socket that accepts, never replies).
Document the framing protocol in 5 lines — that's your wire spec.

labs.title: Resilient HTTP Client
labs.objective: Build an HTTP client with pooling, timeouts, retries, and idempotency.
steps: Shared httpx.Client with limits and (connect, read) timeouts; benchmark vs per-request clients.
Add jittered exponential retry for idempotent methods (GET) with 429/5xx handling (respect Retry-After).
Add idempotency keys for POSTs; build a toy server that dedupes (prove no double-charge on retry).
Test against failure injection: blackhole, slow-loris, flaky 500s. Record behavior per class.
Write the client as a reusable module with the policy documented.

labs.title: Race Hunt
labs.objective: Write a racy counter, observe the lost updates, then fix it three ways.
steps: Write the naive threaded counter (8 threads × 100k increments); run 5x, record the shortfall variance.
Fix 1: lock around the increment; measure overhead vs naive.
Fix 2: no sharing — thread-local counts, sum at end; measure (fastest).
Fix 3: queue-based aggregation (workers put partials, one aggregator sums).
Write the rule: when is each fix appropriate? Document in the bug ledger.

labs.title: Async Server Under Load
labs.objective: Build an asyncio TCP server, load it, and find the blocking call.
steps: Write an asyncio echo server with a /slow endpoint (await asyncio.sleep).
Load with 500 concurrent clients; measure throughput and p99.
Inject the bug: replace one await asyncio.sleep with time.sleep(2); re-measure (watch everything stall).
Fix, then add a semaphore (max 100 concurrent slow requests) — observe backpressure.
Document: the blocking-call audit checklist for async code.

labs.title: RED Metrics End to End
labs.objective: Instrument a service with RED metrics, scrape with Prometheus, and alert on burn.
steps: Write a toy HTTP service; add Counter (requests by status), Histogram (latency by route).
Expose /metrics; configure Prometheus to scrape it.
Write PromQL: error-rate ratio, p99 latency, request rate. Verify against known load.
Add a burn-rate alert with a runbook; inject errors and watch it fire.
Break it: add a high-cardinality label, watch series explode — then remove it. Feel the lesson.

labs.title: Correlation ID Propagation
labs.objective: Propagate one request ID through two services into structured logs.
steps: Service A: generate request_id at ingress (middleware); include in all log records (ctx).
Service A → B: forward via header; B extracts, includes in its logs.
Generate a failing request; query both services' logs by the single ID.
Break propagation (drop the header); observe the debugging cost — document it.
Add the ID to traces/metrics exemplars; verify the three-pillar join.

labs.title: The Composable Tool
labs.objective: Build a CLI honoring the stream contract, exit codes, and machine output.
steps: Write a log-analysis CLI (Typer): subcommands scan/stats, --format table|json, --dry-run for the destructive prune.
Verify: stdout is pure JSON with --format json (pipe to jq); progress goes to stderr.
Verify: exit codes (0 ok, 1 error, 2 usage) — test each path.
Verify: --help documents every flag; a new user can operate it unaided.
Get a peer to use it cold; fix every confusion they hit.

labs.title: Config Precedence + Distribution
labs.objective: Implement the full config chain and distribute the tool two ways.
steps: Implement flags > env > file > defaults with startup validation and --show-effective-config.
Secrets via env/file only; verify no --password flag exists (grep).
Package: pyproject [project.scripts] entry point; install in a fresh venv and run.
Also build a zipapp; run it on a machine without the venv.
Document the install matrix: which artifact for which fleet.

labs.title: Fail-Fast Config System
labs.objective: Build the full config chain with validation that catches every typo.
steps: Implement flags > env > file > defaults with pydantic validation (strict: reject unknown keys).
Feed 10 bad configs (typos, wrong types, out-of-range, missing required); verify each fails at startup with a clear error.
Add --show-effective-config; verify it names the winning source per key.
Add a secret reference (vault://...); verify the value never appears in the config file or logs.

labs.title: Environment Parity Check
labs.objective: Prove stage matches prod's schema, then diff their values safely.
steps: Create stage and prod configs with the same schema, different values.
Write the parity check: same keys, valid values per env, no extras — run in CI.
Break parity deliberately (extra key in prod); watch CI fail with the key named.
Diff effective configs; classify each diff as expected (endpoint) or bug.
Add the check to the deploy pipeline: parity gates promotion.

labs.title: Profile and Fix for Real
labs.objective: Take a slow script through the full discipline: benchmark, profile, fix, verify.
steps: Write (or take) a slow script with a realistic workload; build a benchmark harness (time.perf_counter, multiple runs).
Profile with cProfile (cumulative sort); identify the true bottleneck — write down your pre-profile guess first.
Apply ONE fix (complexity change preferred); re-benchmark. Record the speedup.
Check Amdahl: was the fix on the dominant fraction? Would a second fix be worth it?
Write the report: guess vs reality, fix, speedup, stop-condition check.

labs.title: Memory Leak Hunt

steps: Write a service with a subtle leak (unbounded listener list, cache without maxsize).
Run under load; observe monotonic memory growth (psutil or /proc).
tracemalloc: snapshot, load, snapshot, diff — identify the growing allocation.
Fix with a size policy (bounded structure, weakrefs, explicit cleanup); verify flat memory.

Extend discussion (not code): distributed version (Redis+Lua), clock skew, testing.

steps: Pick three incidents (real or from this course): a deadlock, a leak, a slowdown.
For each, write the 5-minute narrative: symptom → hypothesis → test → found → fix → prevent.

simulations.title: The deadlocking pipeline
simulations.brief: A Python wrapper around ffmpeg hangs forever on large files; small files work fine. Find the plumbing bug.

steps.symptom: The wrapper hangs forever on large inputs; small inputs complete.
evidence:
p = Popen(['ffmpeg', ...], stdin=PIPE, stdout=PIPE)
p.stdin.write(big_blob)
out = p.stdout.read()  # hangs here
ffmpeg blocked writing to a full pipe; parent blocked reading before it finishes writing
options: Use p.communicate(input=big_blob) — it pumps both directions concurrently
Write first, then read, in that order
steps.explain: Classic pipe deadlock: both sides block waiting on each other. communicate() handles the concurrent pumping for you.

steps.symptom: communicate() fixed the hang. Now stderr fills its pipe on noisy inputs and it hangs again.
evidence: p = Popen(..., stdout=PIPE)  # stderr inherits the terminal pipe, unbounded
options: Capture stderr too (stderr=PIPE) and let communicate() drain both, or redirect it to DEVNULL
Read stderr in a thread manually
steps.explain: Every PIPE you open is a pipe you must drain. communicate() drains stdout and stderr together; an undrained stderr re-creates the same deadlock.

steps.symptom: Robust now. The interviewer asks how you would run 50 of these concurrently.
options: A bounded asyncio semaphore around run-in-executor subprocess calls — concurrency with backpressure
One at a time to be safe
steps.explain: Subprocesses are already separate processes; the limit you need is on how many run at once. A semaphore gives throughput with backpressure.

simulations.debrief: Subprocess bugs are plumbing bugs: every PIPE gets drained, communicate() pumps both ways, and concurrency gets a bound.

simulations.title: The leaking event loop
simulations.brief: The logs fill with 'Task was destroyed but it is pending' after every deploy. Trace the abandoned tasks.

steps.symptom: Logs fill with 'Task was destroyed but it is pending' after every deploy.
evidence: Task was destroyed but it is pending! task=<fetch(url)> ×400
options: Track every created task and await them (asyncio.gather / TaskGroup) so none is abandoned
steps.explain: Fire-and-forget tasks are leaks: un-awaited coroutines hold their whole call stack. Structured concurrency (TaskGroup) makes abandonment impossible by construction.

steps.symptom: Tasks are gathered. Now shutdown hangs: tasks ignore cancellation.
options: Re-raise CancelledError after cleanup (or shield only the cleanup) — cancellation must propagate
steps.explain: Swallowed cancellation is a shutdown hang. Cleanup runs, then the CancelledError must propagate so the task actually dies.

steps.symptom: Clean shutdown. How do you prove no task leaks in CI?
options: Assert asyncio.all_tasks() is empty (minus the test task) at the end of the integration test
steps.explain: The loop knows its tasks. Asserting the set is empty after the workload turns the leak into a failing test.

simulations.debrief: Asyncio leaks are abandoned tasks: structure them, propagate cancellation, and assert the loop is empty.

simulations.title: The package that would not install
simulations.brief: pip install succeeds, but the CLI command is missing and its data file is gone. Two packaging bugs, one install.

steps.symptom: pip install works, but the `fetch` command is not found after install.
options: Add [project.scripts] fetch = 'fetch_tool.cli:main' so the installer creates the console script
Tell users to run python -m fetch_tool
Add the script to PATH manually
steps.explain: Console scripts are metadata: without [project.scripts] the installer builds no executable. The entry point maps the command name to a callable.

steps.symptom: Entry point added; the command runs but crashes: FileNotFoundError for config/defaults.yaml.
evidence: config/defaults.yaml sits next to the source, not in the wheel
options: Ship it as package data and load via importlib.resources — no filesystem assumptions
Read it from the source checkout path
Require users to create the file
steps.explain: Wheels only contain declared package data. importlib.resources reads data files portably from installed packages.

steps.symptom: Installs cleanly everywhere. The interviewer asks about version pinning for a CLI tool.
evidence: end users install the CLI directly
options: Pin in a lockfile for reproducible dev/CI, but keep install_requires ranges loose for library consumers
steps.explain: Applications pin for reproducibility; libraries range for compatibility. A CLI is an application — lock it, but do not force pins on downstream importers.

simulations.debrief: Packaging bugs are metadata bugs: entry points create commands, package-data ships files, and importlib.resources finds them.

simulations.title: The GIL-bound batch job
simulations.brief: Hashing 10k images with 8 threads is no faster than serial. The profiler points at the GIL — pick the right tool.

steps.symptom: Hashing 10k images with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) is no faster than serial.
options: Use ProcessPoolExecutor — CPU-bound bytecode needs separate processes to escape the GIL
steps.explain: Threads share the GIL; CPU-bound Python bytecode serializes. Processes each get their own interpreter and GIL — that is what the pool is for.

steps.symptom: ProcessPoolExecutor crashes: Can't pickle local function.
options: Move the worker to module top level — pickle needs an importable qualified name
steps.explain: Multiprocessing ships work by pickling; pickle references functions by module path. Closures and lambdas have no importable name.

steps.symptom: Works. But process startup dominates on small batches.
evidence: process spawn ~300ms each; small batches slower than serial
options: Reuse one long-lived pool and set a chunksize so scheduling overhead stays below the work
Spawn a fresh pool per batch
steps.explain: Process pools amortize spawn cost across the batch; chunksize amortizes scheduling cost across items. Both knobs exist for exactly this.

simulations.debrief: The GIL decides the tool: threads for I/O waiting, processes for CPU burning, and pickle-able top-level functions for the pool.

simulations.title: The 40-minute CLI
simulations.brief: A log-grepping CLI takes 40 minutes on a 2 GB file. Profile it, fix the dominant cost, and know when to stop.

steps.symptom: The log-grepping CLI takes 40 minutes on a 2 GB file.
evidence: 80% of time in re.compile — called once per line

for line in f:
    if re.compile(pattern).search(line): ...
options: Compile the regex once outside the loop
Read the file in bigger chunks first
steps.explain: Profile first, then fix the hotspot: compiling the same pattern 10M times is pure waste. One compile outside the loop removes 80%.

steps.symptom: Down to 8 minutes. The profile now shows 70% in f.readline().
evidence: 70% in readline; per-line Python overhead dominates
options: Read in chunks (or mmap) and split in Python — fewer interpreter round-trips per byte
Read line by line but faster
steps.explain: Per-line I/O syscalls and Python-level looping cost more than the work. Chunked/mmap reads move the splitting into C.

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
